bodyOriginal.text: New York creative agency Basura and musician Big Data have collaborated on a stuffed toy that resembles a data centre and emits a recording from a data centre in Virginia when squeezed.
The stuffed toy, called Bezzy, is part of a larger satirical campaign that draws attention to the impact of data centres and AI as part of the launch of Big Data 's first album in over seven years.

Basura and musician Big Data have collaborated on a stuffed data-centre toy Basura founder Rajeev Basu said the team interviewed "dozens" of people living near data centres for the project and eventually shaped it into the Adopt a Data Centre campaign that includes a website, stickers, posters and Bezzy.
Overall, it imagines "AI data centers as rescue animals looking for their forever homes" according to Basura, informed by initiatives such as WWF's Adopt-a-Panda .

It emits a recording of the hum from a data centre Basu said the toy and campaign were meant to show the absurdity of the data centre building boom, driven by AI, which has led to noise complaints from communities near the functioning data centres.
" Adopt A Data Center is an absurd and provocative invitation to look more closely at what we're being asked to welcome into our lives," Basu told Dezeen.
Read: First images of Gensler-designed 60-building data centre development in Utah revealed The toy is handmade, with a soft body that depicts a data centre, a smile, eyes, and long legs and arms.
When it's squeezed, it emits a recording taken by one of the team's interviewees, a woman who lives by a data centre in Virginia.
"Hug me for ear piercing forever hum," reads a tag on Bezzy.

The toy is part of a wider campaign from the team that seeks to bring attention to the impact of data centres Basu said the interviews were prompted by the desire to understand what living near a data centre "actually feels like".
"The experiences varied, but the same concerns kept coming up: noise, light, changes to the land use and implications for local residents, and demands on local water and electricity," he said.
There are a total of 20 Bezzy toys as part of the release of Big Data's EP 4.0.
The team said the project is " not anti-AI, or anti-technology" but rather seeks to prompt questions about how AI is used responsibly.
"When the promises are so enormous, from transforming everyday life to shaping the future of humanity, the commitment to safety and accountability needs to be just as substantial," said Basu.

Massive data centres are currently being built around the world to support AI models and use large amounts of energy and water on top of the massive land usage. A recently announced hyperscale data centre for AI in Utah will have as much as 10,000 acres dedicated to the facilities.
Recently, residents from around Memphis, Tennessee, sued businessman Elon Musk over the noise pollution, reported NPR .
And beyond sound, scientists have released preliminary studies that point to a pronounced heat island effect as a result of data centre development .

bodyOriginal.text: The major neurodegenerative conditions are characterized by pathology deriving from a small number of misfolded or otherwise altered proteins. Amyloid-β misfolding and aggregation is thought to be the initiating event in Alzheimer's disease , which leads to the spread of altered forms of tau protein that cause the real damage. α-synuclein , once misfolded, spreads from cell to cell through the nervous system like a prion , encouraging other molecules of α-synuclein to also misfold in the same way. Once in the brain, α-syncuclein pathology gives rise to Parkinson's disease . In recent years, researchers have connected the spread of misfolded TDP-43 in the brain to a number of conditions such as frontotemporal dementia . All of these pathologies exist in aged brains to some degree, overlapping and driving dysfunction, and eventually that dysfunction will rise to the level of a named neurodegenerative condition, absent some other form of mortality cutting that process short.

As the past few decades of efforts to develop anti-amyloid therapies for Alzheimer's disease had demonstrated, the biochemistry of protein aggregates and their pathology is enormously complex and remains incompletely understood, even for amyloid-β, even after years of enormous funding for research and development. Amyloid-β clearance took decades to achieve, but does not produce the sizable benefits hoped for in patients , and the reasons why this is the case are yet to be established. It seems likely that the road ahead will be similarly challenging for the development of ways to target other common protein aggregates in the brain. With that in mind, today's open access paper is a tour of the state of development of therapies targeting tau protein aggregation in the aging brain; very different from past anti-amyloid therapy development at the detail level, but quite similar in many ways at the high level.
Therapeutic Targeting of Tauopathies: From Druggable Biology to Precision Intervention

Tauopathies comprise a group of neurodegenerative disorders caused by abnormal tau pathology, including Alzheimer's disease (AD) , frontotemporal dementia (FTD) , progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) , etc. Despite the wide spectrum of tau-related diseases, therapeutic strategies directly targeting pathological tau remain relatively underdeveloped, and no broadly effective clinical treatment has yet to be established.

Most current tau-directed therapeutic approaches have been designed around the tau pathological cascade. Microtubule-associated protein tau (MAPT) mutations and other disease-associated processes can promote abnormal post-translational modifications (PTMs) of tau, with hyperphosphorylation being the most characteristic. Aberrantly modified tau loses microtubule -binding and stabilizing functions, aggregates into neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs) , and ultimately contributes to neuronal dysfunction and degeneration. Based on the pathological mechanism, existing therapeutic strategies can be broadly classified into three categories: (1) reducing overall tau levels at both the RNA and protein levels, (2) regulating tau modifications, and (3) interfering with tau aggregation.

However, these approaches have not achieved satisfactory clinical outcomes, probably due to the complexity of tau pathology. Pathological tau can also spread between neurons , thereby facilitating the propagation of neurodegeneration. In addition, tau interacts with other pathogenic proteins, such as amyloid-β (Aβ) and α-synuclein (α-syn), creating mutually reinforcing pathological cycles that accelerate disease progression. Furthermore, tau exhibits remarkable isoform diversity, beyond abnormalities in protein structure and total amount, an imbalance in tau isoform ratios can itself drive disease development.

In this review, we summarize recent advances focusing on these challenges. Emerging therapeutic strategies are not only targeting more precise molecular sites, but are also placing greater emphasis on co-pathogenic proteins and the broader pathological processes involved in tauopathies. Moreover, by deepening our understanding of tau pathological mechanisms, we propose several potential therapeutic targets that may offer new directions for future drug development and therapeutic strategies for tau-related diseases.

“We are also proud to recognize Steve Totzke for his longstanding commitment to mentorship, inclusion, and the advancement of women across our industry,” Cross and Arocho note. “Together with this year’s winners, they represent the innovation, leadership, and community at the heart of WiT.”

bodyOriginal.text: Chicago-based PBS member station WTTW will be bringing back its documentary series Chicago Stories this fall. One of the four new episodes this season will focus on the city’s toy industry history, appropriately titled “Toy Town.”

The hour-long documentary airs Oct. 9 at 8 p.m. (CST) and focuses on Chicago’s role as a leader in toy innovation and how the city’s toy designers helped create toys that support children’s entertainment and skill development.
Topics include Chicago’s forgotten predecessor to LEGO blocks, the Beanie Baby collection craze, and how the city’s innovators reinvented the industry.
RELATED Toys “R” Us to Wrap the Holiday Season with 120 New Stores

WTTW President and CEO Sandra Cordova Micek shares her thoughts on the new season: “Chicago’s history is not one story, but many — shaped by people, ideas, ambitions, and experiences that continue to influence the city we know today. With this new season of Chicago Stories , we invite viewers to look more closely at the familiar, discover what they may not know, and see our city and our shared history with fresh eyes.”
Viewers can learn more about the docuseries and find out when episodes will air by visiting schedule.wttw.com/series/38107/Chicago-Stories/ .

bodyOriginal.text: FAO Schwarz is bringing its iconic toy store experience to Amazon.com this fall with the launch of its first-ever official Amazon storefront . The new online destination gives U.S. shoppers access to an assortment of toys and gifts from the New York City-based retailer, including timeless favorites and new discoveries.

“FAO Schwarz has sparked joy and wonder for toy lovers around the world for more than 160 years, and we’re thrilled to bring their iconic assortment to Amazon’s stores,” shares Anne Carrihill, Director of Toys and Home at Amazon . “Whether shopping for a birthday, a holiday, or just because, customers now have an even more convenient way to discover this heritage brand.”

The launch also includes a seasonal collaboration between FAO Schwarz and Amazon. A dedicated Amazon pop-up shop will be featured at the FAO Schwarz flagship store at Rockefeller Center, where shoppers can discover toys and gifts featured on Amazon’s 2026 Top 100+ Toys List . The FAO Schwarz windows have also received a seasonal refresh featuring Amazon displays.
RELATED Amazon Reveals Its 2026 Top 100 Toys List

The FAO Schwarz Amazon storefront features a variety of toys and gifts, including plush, baby dolls, musical instruments, and toys designed for play, creativity, and imagination. The online store extends FAO Schwarz’s retail presence beyond its physical locations, giving families another way to shop its collections.

“FAO Schwarz has always been about more than shopping; it’s about creating moments of discovery and wonder,” said David Niggli, Chief Merchandising Officer at FAO Schwarz . “…Bringing FAO Schwarz to Amazon allows us to extend that magic to families everywhere, while our New York flagship continues to deliver the kind of in-person experience that has made FAO Schwarz an iconic destination for generations.”
FAO Schwarz has operated as a toy destination in New York City since 1862. The brand’s global retail presence now includes locations in New York, Paris, Milan, and Beijing.

bodyOriginal.text: A group of five New York artists has created Lifeline, a tote bag that can convert into a self-inflating life jacket as a conceptual design object meant to bring awareness to the threat of climate change -related flooding.
Timed to New York Climate Week, the as-yet-unnamed group used a standard nylon life jacket to create the object, which is meant to be conceptual and is not for sale.

Driven by the recent flooding in the New York City subway system, Lifeline was designed to be a commentary on consumer fashion and on the emergencies of climate change by contrasting the everyday design of a functional tote bag with the emergency design of a life jacket.

bodyOriginal.alt: Lifeline conceptual design

bodyOriginal.text: Lifeline is a tote bag that converts into a life jacket Central to the commentary is the absurdity that such an item needs to exist, or makes sense in context.
"The overarching principle for this project is an essential that shouldn't exist," group member and creative director Phil Le Brun told Dezeen.
"It's an inquiry into conditions and the world which gave rise to this object."

bodyOriginal.alt: Lifeline conceptual design

bodyOriginal.text: It was created to bring awareness to the climate emergency According to designer Gabriela Mestriner, who worked on the project, the final product includes three yards of nylon, polyester zippers, cording and metal locks, most of which came from a deconstructed life vest.
The material was then heat-welded back together.
A zipper that runs through the centre of the bag flap and through the body opens to allow for a person's head to pass through. The set up includes a detached rain hood that can be stored in the bag.

Similar to a regular life jacket, the Lifeline is inflated by pulling on straps. Le Brun said that in testing, they were able to pull off the conversion from tote bag to life jacket in around 15 seconds.

bodyOriginal.alt: Lifeline conceptual design

bodyOriginal.text: It was made using nylon from a standard life jacket Important to the project was what Le Brun calls the "language of emergency" seen in the orange of the final and the inflation mechanism.

However, the styling and photoshoot around the design also helped in the communication of the concept behind the design, with the group working to present the bag in photography that appears almost glamorous.

bodyOriginal.alt: Lifeline conceptual design

bodyOriginal.text: Both the tote bag and life jacket are functional Le Brun said that they were aware of this perception and wanted to lean into it.

"The contrast of normality and then emergency, that juxtaposition and that friction, was deliberate," he said. "It was a deliberate choice for the bag to look kind of cool and normal and be actually functional."
The fact that the life jacket is "hidden" within the bag is a direct commentary on what the group sees as the negative effects of consumerism.
"Hidden within our style and our fashion and our consumerism is a fucking emergency," Le Brun said.

Read: Tian & Teague creates home decor informed by the "discomforts" of New York On the other hand, the photoshoot features images of the bag being converted into a life jacket in the subway, an eerie look into its potential usefulness.
When asked how the message of the design would impact people, Le Brun emphasised the media around it as an important aspect of getting the point across and called it a "narrative object".
"I like to think of it as a narrative object," he said. "I want it to be something that sparks people to think about the choices they make."

bodyOriginal.alt: Lifeline conceptual design

bodyOriginal.text: The group that created Lifeline called it an "essential that shouldn't exist" Lifeline is the group's debut concept and Le Brun said they hope to continue exploring ideas through design.
Other conceptual designs include the Bliss Couch , which creative agency Mother made to function as a life raft.
In Sweden, developer Riksbyggen and creative agency BBDO Nordics created scale apartments based on what young people can afford to highlight the country's housing unaffordability.

bodyOriginal.text: Chinese designer Bin Wu has unveiled the Pavilion of Time, which features timber screens topped by a circular mirror, in the courtyard of Domaine National du Palais-Royal for Paris Design Week .
Wu described the pavilion , which he created in response to the theme of this year's Paris Design Week , Pulse in Motion, as "making time tangible and walkable".

bodyOriginal.alt: Pavilion of Time by Bin Wu

bodyOriginal.text: The pavilion is located in the courtyard of Domaine National du Palais-Royal Beneath its circular roof, the pavilion is divided into three timber segments, each of which has an opening to allow visitors to walk through them in a circle.
Wu wrapped the timber structure in a translucent, paper‑like membrane to allow natural sunlight into the structure and let visitors perceive the movement of time through the shifting light.

bodyOriginal.alt: Pavilion of Time by Bin Wu

bodyOriginal.text: It was designed by interior designer Bin Wu "We hope people move continuously – footsteps trace the arc, sunlight drifts through paper and mirror, wandering between ground and structure," Wu said.
"Light and shadow become intangible hands, inscribing time's trajectory. Here, time is measured not by clocks, but by light; not in numbers, but through the body's motion and repose."

bodyOriginal.alt: Pavilion of Time by Bin Wu

bodyOriginal.text: The structure is wrapped in a translucent paper-like membrane According to Wu, the circular form of the pavilion was designed to contrast the orthogonal classical architecture of the Domaine National du Palais-Royal, while also referencing the ancient Chinese concept of "a round heaven and a square earth".
Its light, translucent design was also deliberately created in juxtaposition to the perceived heaviness of the surrounding historical architecture.
The paper-like membrane that covers the pavilion is made of polyethylene, suitable for outdoor use and resembles the texture of traditional Chinese Xuan paper.

Read: Uchronia installs giant floral sculpture at Grand Palais for Paris Design Week Wu used products from Chinese brands for the pavilion, including a lighting system developed by Chinese smart home brand Moorgen .
This casts a soft light through the translucent walls and allows the pavilion to be lit up at night.
Carbon fibre chairs from Chinese furniture brand Shang Xia were placed at the outer edges of the pavilion, inviting visitors to pause and rest.

bodyOriginal.alt: Pavilion of Time by Bin Wu

bodyOriginal.text: Wu designed a mirrored roof that reflects the surrounding landscape Overall, Wu aimed for the pavilion to give visitors an insight into an Eastern way of experiencing time.
"Eastern time is not a straight line, but a series of perceivable moments," Wu said.
"The Pavilion of Time takes this as its impetus, combining Chinese painting's shifting perspective and temporality to let the body perceive spatial and temporal change."

bodyOriginal.alt: Pavilion of Time by Bin Wu

bodyOriginal.text: At night, light filters through the translucent walls Wu is the founder of interior studio W Design , which was recognised as interior designer of the year at Dezeen Awards China 2024 .
He recently published a book titled The Design Language of Timeless East , exploring the idea of a design language rooted in the philosophical context of the East.
Elsewhere at Paris Design Week, French design studio Uchronia designed a giant floral sculpture at Grand Palais museum .
The Pavilion of Time is on show from 10 to 17 September at Domaine National du Palais-Royal, Paris. See Dezeen Events Guide for more design events, exhibitions and installations around the world.

bodyOriginal.text: Atherosclerosis , the growth of fatty plaques in blood vessel walls, is the largest cause of human mortality. Unstable plaques rupture to block blood vessels to cause a heart attack or stroke , while the narrowing of arteries by plaque contributes to heart failure , dementia , and other conditions. A plaque is in essence a growing macrophage graveyard. Macrophage cells of the innate immune system constantly arrive from the bloodstream, drawn to the plaque, and attempt to repair it. The macrophages are instead overwhelmed by the toxic plaque environment, become inflammatory to call in more macrophages, and die to add their mass to the plaque. The largest plaques also distort the biochemistry of the smooth muscle surrounding blood vessels, and smooth muscle cells transform into macrophages to further accelerate the process of plaque growth - almost a cancer-like mechanism of growth.

Atherosclerosis , the fundamental pathological basis of most cardiovascular diseases which remain the leading cause of global mortality, is driven by both lipid accumulation and dynamic cellular reprogramming within the vessel wall. Central to this process is the remarkable phenotypic plasticity of vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) . Far from being terminally differentiated , VSMCs undergo profound transitions from a contractile state to diverse states, including synthetic, macrophage-like, foam cell -like, and fibroblast -like states, which critically influence plaque formation, stability, and rupture.

This review synthesizes the multilayered molecular mechanisms governing VSMC plasticity, encompassing transcriptional networks, epigenetic reprogramming, and microenvironmental cues. Moreover, this review highlights recent breakthroughs enabled by single-cell omics and lineage tracing , that have revealed unprecedented heterogeneity and clonal expansion of VSMCs within atherosclerotic lesions . Furthermore, we explore the translational potential of targeting VSMC plasticity, and discuss emerging strategies, including phenotype-specific modulation, immunotherapy , nanomedicine , and senotherapeutics .

Finally, we outline future directions focused on dynamic regulatory networks, spatial pathophysiology , and the integration of aging biology to advance precision medicine in atherosclerosis. In summary, VSMC phenotypic plasticity is a core mechanism underlying the initiation and progression of atherosclerosis. Precise modulation of this process holds promise for overcoming current therapeutic limitations and driving a paradigm shift toward mechanism-guided personalized therapy for cardiovascular diseases.

bodyOriginal.text: From laser-cut steel to melted polystyrene waste, 10 designers have reinterpreted the humble hanging basket for a London Design Festival exhibition curated by design gallery Slancha .
Dangling chains and elaborate 3D-printed cups also feature among the 10 hanging baskets displayed in the Hackney studio of fashion agency and retailer Awaykin .

bodyOriginal.alt: Romain Basile Petrot for Slancha

bodyOriginal.text: Romain Basile Petrot's basket is engraved with David Bowie lyrics The brief set by Slancha founders Harvey Everson and Findlay MacDonald was to reconsider the hanging basket – a suspended planter typically used for growing flowers – as a collectable design object.
"We invited 10 contemporary designers to work from the same loose framework of bracket, suspension and vessel, interpreting it through their own materials and practices," MacDonald told Dezeen.

bodyOriginal.alt: ThisIsByron for Slancha Hanging Baskets

bodyOriginal.text: ThisIsByron created a set of hand-carved, aluminium tubes "We selected designers that work across a range of materials, so we knew that the outcomes would all be completely different," he continued.
"It means we have all ends of the spectrum in the show, from really beautiful, small, refined pieces, to larger, more grotesque ones that are somehow beautiful and ugly at the same time."

bodyOriginal.alt: Nicolas Zanoni and for Martha McGuinn for Slancha

bodyOriginal.text: Nicolas Zanoni used polystyrene, while Martha McGuinn worked with steel Among the more abnormal pieces is Pyrofoam Planter by French designer Nicolas Zanoni , a wall-hung basket made by melting industrial polystyrene waste so that it takes on an organic, caramelised form.

Another is Tri-diatreta by London-based Coline Le Quenven , a steel armature that supports three 3D-printed cups, combining references that include Roman cage cups and the neo-Greek bronze furniture of France's Villa Kérylos.
"It's so close to what a traditional hanging basket bracket would be like, but then there's the use of 3D printing, which creates these incredible patterns on the outside," said MacDonald.

bodyOriginal.alt: Tri-diatreta by London-based Coline Le Quenven by Slancha Hanging Baskets

bodyOriginal.text: Coline Le Quenven's design features a trio of suspended 3D-printed cups Romain Basile Petrot was one of three designers to put a twist on a single suspended basket, using stacked plates of aluminium engraved with the lyrics of David Bowie's Space Oddity.

Marc Sweeney paired a recycled champagne bucket from his Pylon series with a fine stainless-steel ball chain, while Martha McGuinn of Jamps Studio used laser cutting to recreate forms found in medieval manuscripts and gothic architecture.

bodyOriginal.alt: Hanna Fastrich for Slancha Hanging Baskets

bodyOriginal.text: Hanna Fastrich created a red-glazed ceramic cross Hanna Fastrich pushed the brief the most in her brutalism-inspired design, Red Hot, a cantilevered arrangement of two slab-built ceramic blocks with a deep red glaze and a small conical dish for flowers.
"The texture is incredible; it almost looks like the bark of a tree," suggested MacDonald.

bodyOriginal.alt: Six Dots for Slancha Hanging Baskets

bodyOriginal.text: Six Dots Design used aluminium to produce the smallest of the baskets The smallest works come from Six Dots Design and ThisIsByron , who both created tubular aluminium forms, while Sheyang Li created a larger but more delicate piece featuring an ash wood hook, a stone support, an aluminium tube and a suspended ceramic vase.

Completing the series is a design by London studio All Ears . It features four vases held inside a striped wooden block, made from alternating layers of maple and walnut, while chains hang down like stems.
The baskets were styled with floral arrangements by Glasgow-based Studio Kumari , featuring dark purple lilies, thistles and yellow tomatoes.

bodyOriginal.alt: Sheyang Li for Slancha Hanging Baskets

bodyOriginal.text: Sheyang Li created a carefully weighted piece using various materials Slancha was recently named on Dezeen as one of five galleries injecting renewed energy into the London design scene .
This show comes a year after the Scottish duo presented the LDF exhibition, The Car Boot Sale , which established their reputation.

MacDonald said the duo felt the best way to follow up the success was to do something completely different this year. In addition to Hanging Baskets, the pair have also created an exhibition and a curated pop-up shop at The Hoxton hotel.

bodyOriginal.alt: All Ears and Marc Sweeney for Hanging Baskets

bodyOriginal.text: Chains feature in the designs of both All Ears and Marc Sweeney "We were quite nervous to come back this year, because we knew everything was going to be a comparison to last year," he said. "We wanted something incomparable to last year, but equally fun in its narrative."

bodyOriginal.text: Chiselled acoustic foam, hand-bent metal and interlocking rulers feature in an exhibition of stools created with single tools, presented by students from the Royal College of Art at London Design Festival .
One Tool, One Stool is the culmination of an exercise undertaken by every design products master's student at the Royal College of Art (RCA).

bodyOriginal.alt: One Tool, One Stool

bodyOriginal.text: One Tool, One Stool is an exhibition by students from the RCA, and includes a foam stool by Pil Gyu Jan As the exhibition title suggests, each student was challenged to conceive a stool using a single tool and minimal materials.

Twenty-three of the varied results are on display at The Lavery in South Kensington, arranged across the floor like precious artefacts within the workspace of the venue's namesake, the late painter John Lavery.

bodyOriginal.alt: Stools by RCA students

bodyOriginal.text: Sue Ye has designed a seat made from paint rollers Ranging from practical to more abstract examples, each stool features a different design. Among the pieces is a low-slung seat by Sue Ye , formed from orange and yellow paint rollers strung together with thin red rope.
Close by is a dusty pink stool by Pil Gyu Jan , made of slabs of acoustic foam that were subtly chiselled into shape.

bodyOriginal.alt: Anisa Yelek-designed candle stool

bodyOriginal.text: Among the more experimental stools is a piece made of candles by Anisa Yelek (pictured at the back) Mayank Patole has crafted a simple, eight-pronged stool out of 10 stainless steel 6o-centimetre rulers. The experimental stool is held together by a single nut and bolt and was created to highlight how a set of measuring tools can become a load-bearing structure.

Considering the exhibition concept, the RCA said, "the exercise asks students to consider how much can be achieved with very little, encouraging resourcefulness and a direct relationship between thinking and making".

bodyOriginal.alt: Stools by RCA students at The Lavery

bodyOriginal.text: Each stool features its own design "Each response reveals a different approach to materials, construction and problem-solving," added the university.
Elsewhere in the exhibition, Anisa Yelek is presenting a bulbous stool made from a cluster of white candles melded together using a heat gun.
Read: Collate Lobby curates fictional 1930s hotel suite to launch its first editions collection Yelek wanted to create seating that encouraged quiet contemplation.
"It's a stool that might melt," she said. "It's a seat that asks you to think about what it means to sit, to stay, to burn."
Nymph Mongkolcheep has designed a textured, cubic stool wreathed in wooden beads bound by spindly wire.

bodyOriginal.alt: Wooden stool by RCA student

bodyOriginal.text: One Tool, One Stool is on display until 20 September Next to Mongkolcheep's piece, Vincent Schwarz placed a hand-bent piece of metal that was shaped to provide seating – among the most minimalist stools in the show.
One Tool, One Stool is part of the Perfectly Imperfect exhibition at The Lavery, curated by Alex Tieghi-Walker . The exhibition also includes the second-ever Studio Iron collectible design show .

bodyOriginal.text: Designer Tom Pearson has created industrial furniture pieces with rivets that are both structural and decorative for the 10,000 Rivets collection, on show at APOC Store during London Design Festival .

The line, which is Tom Pearson Studio 's debut furniture and lighting collection, is on show at London's APOC store , where the aluminium pieces function as display cases and tables for contemporary fashion.

bodyOriginal.alt: Metal shelf

bodyOriginal.text: The 10,000 Rivets collection is on show at APOC Pearson, who previously co-founded and co-ran the fabrication workshop Jamps Studio, turned his focus to the modest industrial fixing for 10,000 Rivets.

He also explored different ways to create surface designs on the aluminium sheets through anodising – a process that changes the metal's structure near its surface and creates a water-resistant layer.

bodyOriginal.alt: Metal furniture with rivets

bodyOriginal.text: Pieces include a table, shelves and lamps "The works came from wanting to further my experiments with anodising," Pearson told Dezeen. "The forms are driven by the constraints of the anodising process."
"The acid tanks I have can only accommodate a certain sheet size, and welding anodised aluminium is feasible but messy, hence the riveted construction," he continued.
"I think it's nicer to be led by chance and play than starting with an overarching 'concept'."

bodyOriginal.alt: Close-up of metal shelf

bodyOriginal.text: Pearson's anodising technique created a droplet pattern The designer started to play around with the anodising process because of the difficulties in finishing aluminium designs.
"Anyone who has worked with aluminium knows how much of a nightmare finishing is – you look away, and it's covered in fingerprints," he said.

Read: Studio Iron exhibition is all about chainmail, cowhide and tattooed leather "Anodising is the solution, but it's hard to find a supplier who is happy for you to experiment in the corner," Pearson continued.
"I started anodising parts myself because I wanted to apply the dyes by hand with brushes without aiming for the usual uniform flat colour."

bodyOriginal.alt: Metal sideboard with bag in it

bodyOriginal.text: The furniture is used to display APOC's fashion pieces While Pearson uses a traditional set-up for anodising aluminium, he experimented with different ways of applying dye to the material, using brushes, airbrushes and pipettes.
The resulting patterns look like water droplets, creating a surface design that is both unusual and decorative.
"My setup is no different to the usual process, involving acid and boiling water; I am just treating it as a decorative patina embracing all the unpredictability of the process," Pearson said.

bodyOriginal.alt: Metal shelving

bodyOriginal.text: The 10,000 Rivets collection was unveiled at London Design Festival Pearson's aluminium pieces, which have angular, geometric shapes, are held together by rivets that run along their seams.
This creates a look that makes some of the shelving seem as if it's floating, and gives the shelves, tables, accessories and lighting designs sculptural patterned edges.

bodyOriginal.alt: Riveted table

bodyOriginal.text: Rivets decorate the sides of an aluminium table While the pieces on show feature thousands of rivets, they do not quite make it to the number in the exhibition's name.
"There are technically 6,264 rivets in the works," Pearson said. "I ordered 10,000. Who knows where the rest have gone!"
Other London Design Festival projects on Dezeen include Studio Iron's show featuring chainmail, cowhide and tattooed leather and an exhibition designed as a fictional 1930s hotel suite .
The collection was produced by design consultancy Heavy Duty Services . The photography is by Studio Adamson .

bodyOriginal.text: Promotion: H World has debuted its latest hotel brand, the Grand Ji Hotel, in Hangzhou, China , designed by Chinese studio Vermilion Zhou Design Group, which aims to reinvent hotel design through its dedication to symbolic ritual.

Grand Ji Hotel, a premium brand under H World Group , has made its official debut at Paris Design Week's China Creative Power (CCP) pavilion as an official annual partner, taking place from 10 to 19 September.
The hotel's spatial design was led by Kuang Ming (Ray) Chou, founder and creative director of Vermilion Zhou Design Group and chief designer of H World Group.

bodyOriginal.alt: Grand Ji Hotel

bodyOriginal.text: H World debuted its Grand Ji Hotel during Paris Design Week According to H World, Grand Ji Hotel draws on the phrase "the formless greatness, a quiet way of seeing" and is informed by the Taoist concept of 大象无形, which suggests that the most powerful forms are often "quiet and insular".
Instead of an overtly luxurious look, the hotel's aesthetic is described as "quiet, yet possessed of presence, unlayered, yet full of depth".

bodyOriginal.alt: Grand Ji Hotel

bodyOriginal.text: The technology woven into the design ensures the guest experience is seamless Rather than weaving traditional Chinese imagery throughout the hotel design, Grand Ji Hotel was designed to break the conventional hotel paradigms and instead focus on quietly enhancing visitor experience.
For example, the way guests arrive, dine, rest and depart are treated as part of one integrated system.
When guests arrive, instead of checking in at a large front desk, they are greeted by a tea table where they can first enjoy a tea ceremony and a hot cup of tea.

bodyOriginal.alt: Grand Ji Hotel

bodyOriginal.text: Guests are greeted with a tea ceremony upon arrival At Grand Ji Hotels, technology is integrated purposefully into the background to ensure a smooth experience.
Visitors can use their phones as a room key, and rooms are also fitted with innovative control systems, where curtains, televisions, and air conditioning are controlled via voice commands.
H World explained that the "Eastern spirit" is woven into each room's design, with furniture that evokes a sense of sensory calm and hospitality rituals embedded in the structure.

bodyOriginal.alt: Grand Ji Hotel

bodyOriginal.text: H World Group is one of the world's largest hotel groups Throughout the creative process, the designers also looked to incorporate cultural and natural motifs into the building's spatial qualities.
Here, the materials, art and how light flows through the building were influenced by five Eastern motifs: water, clouds, mountains, pine and tea.
Water symbolises the hotel's flow and calmness, clouds stand for lightness, tea represents zen, mountains signify depth, and pine embodies resilience.

bodyOriginal.alt: Grand Ji Hotel

bodyOriginal.text: The bricks within the hotel entrance wall were made from compressed tea leaves, introducing scent before guests enter the lobby H World explained that its inclusion in Paris Design Week is the first time a Chinese hotel brand has taken part in the week under its own name, which marks a shift from Chinese hotel brands "leading in scale" to "leading in design."
H World added that Grand Ji Hotel's participation also spotlights the Chinese hotel industry's growing force within the international design space.

bodyOriginal.text: Promotion: subtly reflective silver-grey glass and tactile physical controls characterise Fisher & Paykel 's Contemporary Style kitchen appliances , designed with versatility for the social heart of the home.
The Contemporary appliances are one of three product design styles in the New Zealand company's luxury range, alongside the Minimal and Professional offerings.
Fisher & Paykel explained that each of its curated styles supports architects, designers and homeowners in creating bespoke kitchens with a cohesive aesthetic.
"The advantage is a consistent design language across the appliance collection, from cooking and cooling to wine care and dishwashing," said the brand.

Its aesthetic contrasts with the Minimal Style, where dark colours and dial- and handle-free designs allow the products to recede into the background.

Together, the style families are intended to enable the creation of bespoke spaces befitting the evolving role of the domestic kitchen. Fisher & Paykel explained that once hidden from view, kitchens are now one of the main social spaces in the home.
They attract a constant thrum of activity as families join in meal preparation, guests hover and chat, and daily rituals are tended to.

articles.titleOriginal: Clearing Damaged Mitochondria to Fight Skin Photoaging
articles.summaryOriginal: Researchers publishing in Aging Cell have found that a cocktail of molecules released by human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells (hUC-MSCs) can mitigate sun-induced skin aging (photoaging) […]

bodyOriginal.text: Researchers publishing in Aging Cell have found that a cocktail of molecules released by human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells (hUC-MSCs) can mitigate sun-induced skin aging (photoaging) in mice by restoring their cells’ ability to get rid of their own damaged mitochondria (mitophagy).

Wrinkles are only a small part of the problem Chronic exposure to ultraviolet light is the main driver of photoaging, which is characterized by the accumulation of senescent cells in the skin along with the depletion of DNA-protecting lamins [1]. It causes skin to become thickened, wrinkled, and rough while accumulating visible veins [2]. This damage is more than cosmetic; photoaging can lead to precancerous lesions along with cancer itself [3]. Retinoids and other antioxidants have been found to have some effects but cannot completely reverse this damage [4], and laser-based treatments may be expensive and painful while causing other symptoms [5].

This work focuses on the relationship between the accumulation of damaged mitochondria ( mitochondrial dysfunction ) and age-related inflammation in the absence of pathogens ( inflammaging ). Mitochondrial dysfunction leads to the activation of the inflammatory cGAS-STING pathway [6], which increases the production of cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-8 and is known to drive inflammaging in other tissues [7].

The compounds secreted by hUC-MSCs, including proteins and exosomes, are collectively referred to as the secretome, which has been found to treat diabetic skin lesions in a mouse model [8]. Previous work had involved some of these components, and we have reported extensively on the use of exosomes . However, this team utilized the secretome as a whole, attempting to determine the extent of its effects against mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammaging in the context of skin photoaging.

Broad and significant effects The researchers initially ran a mouse experiment in which they shaved patches of skin and exposed the animals to 40 days of UVA and UVB light calibrated to mimic chronic sun exposure, then treated some of the irradiated skin with a topical hUC-MSC-derived secretome. Compared to the control group, the treated mice showed less epidermal thickening, better hydration, improved elasticity, and less water loss through the skin barrier. Skin collagen, which typically fragments and depletes with ultraviolet exposure, was largely preserved as well. Two markers of cellular senescence, p16 and p21, were also reduced in these animals.

The team also irradiated human skin cells (HaCaT keratinocytes) with UVB and cultured some of them in the presence of an MSC-derived secretome. The results were similar to those seen in mice: compared to the control group, the treated cells were less likely to become senescent as measured by the well-known biomarker SA-β-gal, and they had less UV-induced reduction of Lamin B1.

As expected, compared to mice that were never exposed to ultraviolet radiation at all, exposed mice had more dysfunctional mitochondria and a significant reduction in mitophagy; this was evidenced by increases in mitochondrial proteins, a decrease in the mitophagy biomarker LC3B-II, and similar decreases in the related factors PINK1 and Parkin. These researchers found that treatment with the MSC secretome mitigated this dysfunction completely, as markers of functional mitophagy were indistinguishable from those of the UV-unexposed control group, and these findings were also replicated in vitro with HaCaT cells. Similarly, treatment with this secretome reduced activation of cGAS/STING and diminished the production of downstream inflammatory cytokines, both in mouse skin and in cultured cells.

A clear causal chain Mitophagy was confirmed to be the key driver of the hUC-MSC secretome’s effects. Alongside administration of Mdivi-1, which blocks mitophagy, this secretome was found to be ineffective. Directly blocking STING through the H151 inhibitor, or forcing mitophagy through the compound CCCP, had similar effects as secretome administration in vitro . A series of in vivo experiments utilizing combinations of these compounds confirmed this hierarchical relationship: the hUC-MSC secretome induces mitophagy, which fights cGAS/STING-related inflammation, which is responsible for many of the downstream negative effects of photoaging.

Of course, these experiments were conducted with mice and a single immortalized human skin cell line; as human skin is thicker than mouse skin and has likely suffered different long-term damage over a longer lifespan, the results of a clinical trial may be different. These researchers also chose to use the MSC secretome as a whole rather than specific proteins or exosomes, which obfuscates the contributions of its various components.

However, this study confirms that the skin, just like the heart and brain, experiences inflammaging driven by mitochondrial dysfunction. If the particular factors involved in the hUC-MSC secretome’s effects against this dysfunction can be identified, clinically tested, and produced, such a product may be more effective than current treatment methods.

bodyOriginal.text: Canadian studio RHAD Architects has completed Two Bay House in Nova Scotia, Canada, which consists of blocky volumes with carved-out voids, mass-timber framing and blackened wood cladding.
The waterfront home is located within a family estate on Cape Breton Island, in northeastern Nova Scotia .

The design began with two simple masses, which were then strategically carved away to form courtyards , terraces and double-height spaces. These voids were designed to "mediate between shelter and landscape".

bodyOriginal.alt: RHAD House view from lake in Nova Scotia

bodyOriginal.text: RHAD Architects has completed Two Bay house in Nova Scotia "The architecture emerges not through the addition of elements, but through a series of deliberate acts of subtraction and carving," said RHAD Architects , a studio based in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia, and led by founder Rayleen Hill.
"The resulting voids are as significant as the forms themselves, becoming the spaces through which the house is experienced."

bodyOriginal.alt: RHAD Architects Two Bay House

bodyOriginal.text: The house is oriented towards a lake The house rises two levels and is partly made of mass timber. Its primary roof structure consists of glue-laminated timber, while the roof decking is standard lumber.
The walls are made of insulated concrete forms (ICFs).

bodyOriginal.alt: Black house with two window bays

bodyOriginal.text: The project is named after its two parallel volumes In plan, it consists of two parallel bars, or "bays", with one shorter in length.
"Their differing lengths establish a protected, west-facing courtyard that shelters outdoor living from prevailing waterfront winds while capturing afternoon sunlight," the team said.

bodyOriginal.alt: Aerial of RHAD Architects Two Bay house

bodyOriginal.text: One "bay" was made shorter to form protected courtyards Exterior walls are clad in vertical wooden siding that was charred using shou sugi ban (yakisugi), an ancient Japanese technique. Treated with black oil, the burnt wood "gives the building a quiet, monolithic presence within the landscape".
In carved-away areas, the solid charred wood gives way to slatted wood and vertical-grain hemlock siding.

bodyOriginal.alt: RHAD Architects Two Bay house close up exterior

bodyOriginal.text: Most of the house was clad with charred wood "The contrast between charred and natural wood makes each subtraction legible, revealing the spaces where the architecture opens itself to light, landscape and occupation," the team said.
The home is entered on the east, where one finds an entry court enclosed within tall, slatted walls.
Filtered sunlight passes into the threshold, creating changing patterns throughout the day, while the enclosure glows in the evening from internal light.

bodyOriginal.alt: RHAD Architects Two Bay house living room interior

bodyOriginal.text: The longer of the two volumes features the living room The vertical space acts as a "constant point of reference" within the home, the team said.
Inside, there is a division between communal and private areas.
The shorter of the two volumes contains two bedrooms on the bottom level and a primary bedroom up above.
The longer volume holds a kitchen, dining area and living room on the ground floor. Upstairs, there is a music room and a small salon, as one of the clients is a hairstylist.

bodyOriginal.alt: RHAD Architects Two Bay house kitchen

bodyOriginal.text: Interior voids and skylights work to bring light into the interior A large portion of the upper floor is carved away, forming a void in the centre of the house. A loft and glass-walled bridge overlook the communal area, "allowing light, conversation and activity to move freely between levels".

Along the water-facing side of the house, ample glazing and covered terraces extend the interior living spaces outward – "allowing the architecture to project into the landscape while maintaining a strong sense of enclosure", the team said.

bodyOriginal.alt: RHAD ARchitects upper floor

bodyOriginal.text: It was designed to show "how subtraction can generate richness" The west side of the house features a swimming pool surrounded by a generous terrace.
Overall, it was designed to show "how subtraction can generate richness," the studio said.
"Rather than relying on formal complexity, it demonstrates how carefully carved voids can produce moments of compression and release, darkness and light, intimacy and openness.
"The result is a home whose character is defined as much by the spaces removed as by those that remain."

bodyOriginal.text: Italy’s South Tyrol province, which borders Switzerland and Austria in the Alps and is home to some of Central Europe’s most dramatic mountains, lives up to its geographic position as a borderland. Italy annexed the region in 1919 following World War I, prior to which it was part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Many people are German-speaking, and in many ways, their cultural traditions and ancestry lean traditionally toward Austria more than Italy.

At the outbreak of World War II, the Fascist Italian regime built a series of fortifications along the country’s northernmost border. Construction was halted at the onset of the war, and the military controlled what had been completed until 1993. For Vincenzo Pagliuca , these purpose-built structures spurred an intrepid yet pensive body of work called Bunker, published in hardcover by Hartmann Books.

bodyOriginal.alt: a photograph by Vincenzo Pagliuca of a WWII bunker in South Tyrol

bodyOriginal.text: Many of the bunkers are freestanding concrete masses with distinctive domed shapes and thick walls. Others take advantage of the ancient pre-existing stone, sometimes carving directly into mountainsides and augmenting with extra barriers. Over the years, grasses have colonized the roofs, shrubs have grown close, and some of the exteriors, which were designed to camouflage against the slopes like exposed rock, have a surreal, almost Gaudí-esque character.

Pagliuca has long been fascinated by Italian architecture, such as in his project Mónos , which highlights the often quirky vernacular of diminutive homes. For Bunker, he was interested in the relationship of these specific structures to their rarefied and remote locations, their solidity and often hulking presence at odds with the surrounding Alpine meadows and soaring, snow-capped peaks.

These human interventions, depicted without the presence of people, are a permanent reminder of the drastic measures that political and military forces will go in the name of nationalism. “The bunkers represent a difficult legacy, recalling a dramatic historical period in Central Europe marked by nationalist ideology and the inability to resolve conflicts through peaceful means—an era we thought had long since passed,” says a statement from the publisher.

bodyOriginal.text: Damage to nuclear DNA occurs constantly, and near all of it is immediately repaired. A tiny fraction lingers, however, and over time a burden of mutational damage builds up in tissues throughout the body. It is an open question as to how large a component of degenerative aging is a direct result of this damage, under normal circumstances. High rates of mutation in individuals with disabled DNA repair mechanisms shorten life span and accelerate the onset of age-related conditions, sometimes dramatically, but that doesn't necessarily mean the DNA damage is important in aging at levels exhibited in normal individuals. The best approach to firm data is to find a way to suppress or repair mutations without affecting other mechanisms, but the life-extending interventions that are known to slow the accumulation of DNA damage also have many other beneficial effects on metabolism. As reported here, for example, calorie restriction slows the pace at which the burden of DNA damage grows over time. Calorie restriction also improves cell function and health in numerous other ways, however, producing sweeping changes in the operation of cells and systems throughout the body that are unrelated to DNA damage.

Past studies in animals have shown that a large reduction in the number of calories they consume, called caloric restriction, extends their lifespans and slows aspects of aging. But whether caloric restriction also slows the rate at which mutations occur with age had not been investigated across the genome , the complete set of genetic material present in every cell. A new study has shown that caloric restriction reduced the level of mutations across several tissues in mice that were fed 30 percent fewer calories than they would have ingested if allowed to eat freely.

The study analyzed the effect of caloric restriction on different types of genetic changes. They found that to varying degrees across tissues, it dialed down the level of substitution mutations , in which one DNA letter is swapped for another, and insertion and deletion mutations, in which one or more DNA letters are added to or missing from the genome. The study results also showed that the impact of caloric restriction varies across tissues and cell types, as well as across the genome. For example, liver cells showed a greater reduction in mutation burdens with caloric restriction than kidney or brain cells.

Surprisingly, in liver and kidney cells, the reduction in the number of mutations from caloric restriction was greatest in the least-active regions of the genome, which contain either no genes or genes not being used by a given cell. One possible explanation is that if caloric restriction reduces DNA damage across the genome, active regions of the genome would not benefit as much because those regions already repair DNA damage frequently.

bodyOriginal.text: Isamaya Ffrench has opened her second Studio Iron show The project is back for London Design Festival (LDF), on display as part of curator Alex Tieghi-Walker's Perfectly Imperfect programme in the Brompton Design District.
Ffrench selected 27 creatives for the exhibition, featuring pieces that challenge ideas about what materials go together.

bodyOriginal.alt: Cowhide armchair

bodyOriginal.text: Armchairs by Andu Masebo and Thomas Cardiff feature in the show "Our designers are based all over the world, and as someone who's highly into the tactility of objects and art, it was amazing to see all the pieces in real life," she told Dezeen. "To see how they looked, what they felt like, and to witness their scale."
"Most of the time, we get to experience art and design on the internet, in museums or in shops as the finished piece with great lighting and great props," she continued.

"But I'm more interested in the process, the tools, the raw materials, and the industrial machines. It's a real privilege to be in an artist's space and to talk to them about their inspiration or see them at work."

bodyOriginal.alt: Studio Iron by Isamayya Ffrench

bodyOriginal.text: Various contrasting materials make up the pieces Among the selection is a low-slung hammered steel pouf by Jesse Butterfield , topped with a lacy linen cushion by Jane Wright .
Opposite the pouf, an oversized, angular armchair by tattoo artist Thomas Cardiff is on display, crafted from a steel frame with a cowhide-clad seat and tattooed leather sides.

bodyOriginal.alt: Perfectly Imperfect

bodyOriginal.text: They form part of the Perfectly Imperfect exhibition in west London Marten Herma Anderson is showing a bloated resin lamp with a gridded pattern and a nickel-plated brass base, while Atelier Fomenta is presenting a bulb encased in a cylindrical slab of rubber held together with rivets.
A tangled stainless steel coat rack by Andu Masebo was placed in the corner of the gallery, close to a chunky hammered steel mirror, also by Butterfield.

bodyOriginal.alt: Silver ash tray

bodyOriginal.text: Different-sized furniture and objects make up the selection Blacksmith Barnaby Lewis 's spindly, skeletal chair features in the show, alongside a stainless steel floor lamp by Wretched Flowers , cloaked in chainmail, gemstones and glass beads.
Lewis is among the London-based rising talents spotlighted in the Dezeen Dispatch newspaper we published for LDF.
"Barnaby's practice is visceral and poetic at the same time and he's also wildly prolific," Ffrench told Dezeen. "His work deserves more attention."

Read: London has "the best architecture and interior design community in Europe" says Duncan Riches London-based Ffrench said that she hopes to expand Studio Iron, which is still in its infancy, into an interdisciplinary creative agency that champions young designers.
"London feels genuinely open in terms of how people work," said the artist. "There's less pressure to attach yourself to a single practice, which makes it easier to move between disciplines."

bodyOriginal.alt: Studio Iron exhibition

bodyOriginal.text: Rubber and resin were used to create some of the show's lamps "Galleries and shops are also much more inclined to represent and sell the work of emerging artists versus established ones," added Ffrench. "And I think it is vital to support them and help them grow."

Initially conceived as a transportable ski cabin by Finnish architect The post How a Facebook po

bodyOriginal.text: A Matti Suuronen Futuro House has been manufactured for the first time in decades and decked out by Finnish design brand Marimekko for Helsinki Design Week .
The famously flying-saucer-like structure recently landed in Kaisaniemi Botanical Gardens as part of the Finnish capital's annual design festival .
Initially conceived as a transportable ski cabin by Finnish architect Matti Suuronen in 1968, the Futuro House is among the most distinctive emblems of space-age architecture.

bodyOriginal.alt: Futuro House at Helsinki Design Week 2026

bodyOriginal.text: The first new Futuro House for decades made an appearance at Helsinki Design Week. Photo by Justus Hirvi Prefrabricated in fibreglass-reinforced plastic, it was once described by British critic Justin McGuirk as "the closest housing ever came to product design".
Despite being intended for mass production, fewer than 100 were made worldwide. Manufacture ceased shortly after the 1973 oil crisis, which sent the price of plastic rocketing.
Around 60 are estimated to still be in existence, scattered across the globe in varying states of repair.

That number became one greater recently for the first time in decades, thanks to a project that began in 2024 when Dutch-American preservationist architect Jan van Dijs was alerted by a friend and client to an unusual post on Facebook.
An executive at a Finnish materials firm, Exel Composites, was selling the original Futuro moulds.
"How fascinating if we could actually do this"
At this point, Van Dijs, who has spent much of his career restoring mid-century houses in California , was only vaguely familiar with the Futuro Houses.
"I dug in a little bit, I started to learn about the history," he told Dezeen. "And I start to realise that it's something of a fascinating story."

"And I really had my doubts that all the pieces were there, that they could be restored, so I tried to keep all of that in check," he added. "But I certainly had started to make an emotional connection to how fascinating this could be if we could actually do this."
Twenty Futuro Houses had been fabricated in its native Finland originally, by plastics company PolyKem.

Exel had acquired PolyKem's assets, including the Futuro moulds, after the fabricator went bankrupt in the early 1990s – a difficult period for Suuronen that reportedly culminated in him and his wife losing their home.

bodyOriginal.alt: Futuro moulds

bodyOriginal.text: The moulds were in a sorry state when van Dijs first saw them. Photo by Jan van Dijs In the decades since production stopped, the moulds had been periodically moved between various forms of storage without a purpose.
Suuronen died in 2013, and so once hooked on the Futuro story, Van Dijs spent several months trying to engage with the architect's family.

"I couldn't just buy the moulds and build this thing – I needed to have a license, and I needed to have their support," he said. "The reality was, unless I could do that, there was no future for this project."
The Suuronens were hesitant, having been contacted several times over the years about poorly thought-through schemes on a similar theme.
But eventually they were persuaded with help from the Exel man, Jyrki Aho, who died a short while later.
When Van Dijs flew out to see the moulds in May 2025, they were languishing in a field and nearly 60 years old.
"The exterior of the moulds looked like hell," he remembered. "I mean, there was grass growing out of them and moss covering them, and it looked really bad."

Nevertheless, the decision was made to proceed, and Van Dijs worked with Finnish plastic fabrication company Ekin Muovi to restore the moulds and recast the panels with the aim of producing a faithful reconstruction of Suuronen's design.

bodyOriginal.alt: Futuro House moulds

bodyOriginal.text: The pieces had been drifting into decay since the 1970s. Photo by Jan van Dijs Even the same paint colours were used, having been matched from scraps that remained on the moulds.
It was a step into the unknown for Van Dijs, and he admits the process was trickier than he had anticipated.

While today plastic moulding uses two tessellating pieces – one to pour the cast into and one to press over it to squeeze out all the air – Suuronen's are one-part moulds, meaning air bubbles must be eliminated manually.
"It's all hand labour," said Van Dijs. "Nobody does it like that anymore."
Casting a single panel therefore took days instead of hours and was very labour-intensive – "no doubt a large contributor to the problems faced by the Futuro in the 1970s", Van Dijs suggests.

bodyOriginal.alt: Futuro House fabrication

bodyOriginal.text: Casting the new Futuro panels was a painstaking process. Photo by Jan van Dijs There were pleasant surprises as well, however. Unexpectedly, the moulds being sold by Exel included furniture designs by Suuronen, which have also been reproduced as part of the project.
They include built-in lounge chairs, a dining table, and the Orbit chair.

The fabrication process took five months, including some mishaps along the way. Including the restoration of the moulds, Van Dijs estimates the project has cost around 450,000 Euros, though he hopes further Futuros would cost less than 300,000.

In late June of this year, the 21st Futuro House to be made in its native country was completed, ready to be transported in several pieces for reassembly at its temporary home on the Kaisaniemi lawns.

bodyOriginal.alt: Half-built Futuro House

bodyOriginal.text: The new Futuro was manufactured in five months, completing in late June. Photo by Jan van Dijs For the Helsinki Design Week installation, Marimekko was invited to create an interior for the new Futuro House.
It opted to divide the open space into three areas – one for lounging and sleeping, one for eating and working, and a kitchenette.
"It was really important to sort of create a proposal for future ways of living," Marimekko creative director Rebekka Bay told Dezeen.

"That sounds like a big, grand statement, but we were really just intrigued by how we would live in the Futuro House today. I think there is a real trend for downscaling, and we felt that the Futuro House is sort of speaking to that."

bodyOriginal.alt: Marimekko installation at Helsinki Design Week 2026

bodyOriginal.text: Marimekko wanted its Futuro installation to feel "tactile, lived-in". Photo by Justus Hirvi Marimekko products were displayed on perspex shelving units that double as transparent room dividers, while stripy prints created for the brand during a residency by Danish textile artist Vibeke Rohland were used to upholster the furniture.
"It would have been obvious for us, of course, to go back to our archives and find prints that were designed in 1968 when the house was also designed," said Bay.

"But we wanted to take the opposite route and propose something that had been created today. We convey certain images when we speak to the future, but we wanted our proposal to be sort of tactile, lived-in, friendlier, and were therefore intrigued to use brand new textile designs."
With design week over, discussions about the structure's future are now ongoing, though Van Dijs said his preference is for it to remain on public display in Finland.

bodyOriginal.alt: Marimekko Futuro House installation

bodyOriginal.text: The brand's products were displayed on transparent shelving units. Photo by Justus Hirvi "I hope it will move somewhere into the countryside and someone will be using it as their summer cabin," said Bay. "I think that would be wonderful."
Van Dijs also plans to produce new Futuro Houses to order – but the run will be limited.
"Casting moulds are just like the plates for a print; they are designed for a limited number of editions," he said.
"I think the original moulds were probably near the end of their lifespan when production stopped. Through a significant effort we were able to extend their life, but not forever."

Read: "What if houses were designed like bikes?" He estimates that the restored moulds will support producing between four and six new Futuros. After that the moulds will be destroyed, and, in Van Dijs's words, "that will be the end of the original Futuros".
In his design, Suuronen focused on making the Futuro House quick to assemble, quick to heat and suitable for difficult terrains.
But it is also cramped, tricky to transport and dreadfully insulated, leaving it without an obvious practical use in 2026.

bodyOriginal.alt: Futuro House at Helsinki Design Week

bodyOriginal.text: Plans for the Futuro's next home are still being finalised. Photo by Justus Hirvi Nevertheless, Van Dijs is adamant that Suuronen's creation is more than mere whimsy.
"I would love to leave my home every day and go to my Futuro office, a small apartment, yoga studio, architectural book store," he suggested.

He regards the Futuro as an important touchstone for radical post-war optimism and creativity – the same conditions from which Marimekko was born in 1951 – and sees his project as a reigniting of that spirit.
"I think the Futuro should be considered an icon of Finnish design, which was not the case when it was originally produced," he said.
"This project allows us to see the Futuro as Matti Suuronen envisioned it – I think that's important."
Helsinki Design Week took place from 28 August to 6 September in various locations across Helsinki. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

Piloseno The post "Is colour actually architecture?" panellists ask at

bodyOriginal.text: Promotion: in a time of dopamine design and AI tools , a group of design industry professionals at an Arca talk discussed what role colour is playing in the contemporary American home.
Colours such as olive greens and a shade called Black Martini are in, according to Tony Piloseno, owner of Orlando-based company Tonester Paints .
Piloseno joined interior designers Kati Curtis and Tamara Feldman for a conversation at Mexican stone company Arca' s showroom in Miami, moderated by Dezeen US editor Ben Dreith.
And while the panellists agreed that rich, dark colours are in at the moment, the most important element of contemporary colour usage is about experience and reevaluating how people choose colour.

bodyOriginal.alt: Arca Wynwood

bodyOriginal.text: Arca and Dezeen hosted a talk at the Mexican stone company's Wynwood Miami showroom "I use tons of colour in my work, but what I'm thinking about, more so than trends, is how are we using colour?" said Curtis. "Are we using colour as an applied element, or is colour actually architecture?"
Both Curtis and Feldman referenced the work of Mexican modernist architect Luis Barragán in their framing of colour as more than a trendy accent.

"The term colour blocking has always bothered me because I feel like it's an accent – it's like putting wallpaper on one wall," continued Curtis. "It feels to me like you ran out of money, and you just went with that."

bodyOriginal.alt: Dezeen pane

bodyOriginal.text: The panellists included (from left) Ben Dreith, Tamara Feldman, Kati Curtis and Tony Piloseno An expanded conception of colour utilises light, texture, and the aim should be to envelop whoever is in a space. The panellists noted how the presence of tinted glass in Miami makes this even more important.
This, for Feldman, means that the whole of an interior – including light – and all the way through to the artwork on the walls should work together.
"I don't think it's just about a colour and a wall," she said. "I think it's the whole concept together."

Feldman is currently designing a coffee pavilion for the Institute of Contemporary Art in Miami, where she has used mirrors and Arca's Umbria-fabricate tiles to create a sculptural work in the institution's gardens.

bodyOriginal.alt: Tony Piloseno with microphone

bodyOriginal.text: Piloseno spoke on contemporary colour trends and specifying techniques The idea that colour should envelop and create an emotional response has become a hot topic recently, with the emerging trend of so-called "dopamine design" seeing spaces covered in bright colours and mish-mashed patterns to stimulate the mind.

The panellists agreed that colour can work to make you feel at ease, comfortable or inspired, but that this is more related to individual preference and experience than any set configuration or style.

"Does the room look really cool on TikTok, then you hate it 15 minutes later because you threw it in there to try to create this cool picture?" asked Curtis. "It can definitely go in the wrong direction too if you don't know what you're doing."

bodyOriginal.alt: Tamara Feldman

bodyOriginal.text: The panellists agreed on the usefulness of AI but highlighted the personal aspects of colour selection and design Piloseno added that dark colours that wash over you can have a positive effect as well.
"There is a direct emotional impact that colour has, especially with these darker colours," he said.

The panellists also addressed AI in design, and how choosing a colour scheme can be risky. For example, once you apply the paint or veneer, it takes a significant amount of work to pivot in a different direction.
Visualisation tools have existed for years, but Curtis said that generative AI has allowed her to show clients what a space might look like more easily before they commit.

"Even if it's not an accurate representation of exactly what the colour is going to be, I think it's very helpful in giving clients an idea of the overall room rather than just testing a sample," said Curtis.
"What AI and just any kind of colour visualiser tool will help with is seeing the specific colour vertically or how it's going to look on the ceiling with specific shadows," added Piloseno.
Ultimately, though, the panellists agreed that the pursuit of colour, and whatever downstream emotional effects, requires a human touch.
"I think the whole process of selecting colours is very personal," said Piloseno. "You shouldn't have AI guide you to these specific colours."

bodyOriginal.alt: Arca showroom Dezeen talk

bodyOriginal.text: The event brought out a large crowd of Miami professionals The speakers added that personal relationships and understanding the emotions of clients are paramount.
Colour choices often represent this dynamic more than other aspects of design. If a designer is going to understand what will engage the mind, they need to know the mind in question.
"What we do is really part therapy, part design," said Feldman.

Technology underwrites the process while the person guides the choices on the table. And while neuroscience has created new streams for engaging with design schemes, Curtis said that the foundations remain as important as ever.
"As long as you stick with those fundamental elements that we all know, we can mix all of those things in a really beautiful way," added Feldman. "That's going to make everybody's dopamine work."

bodyOriginal.text: A pasta-shaped daybed and speakers that resemble Saturn's rings are among the products on display at Contemporary Design Selections at this year's Lake Como Design Festival .

The eighth edition of the Contemporary Design Selections show, curated by Giovanna Massoni , follows the festival theme of Borders, encouraging participating designers, architects and makers to consider boundaries in design.
The theme could be interpreted through materiality, form, function or design's relation to other disciplines, while the open call also highlighted the social and political elements of the industry.
The exhibition is located at Villa Saporiti, which marks the first public showcase in the neoclassical building, and displays 57 projects by designers and studios from 30 countries.
The showcase features furniture, lighting, functional objects and textiles selected by Massoni across 10 rooms in the villa and its outdoor spaces.
Read on for seven design pieces that caught our attention:

bodyOriginal.alt: Photo of metal and leather chairs by Studio Bjorn Verlinde

bodyOriginal.text: Belgium-based Studio Bjorn Verlinde spotlighted its minimal Fur seating and side table collection at the exhibition.
Designed for restless people, the series features an unconventional backless rocking chair with a curved aluminium base that allows the user to gently lean back.
A contrasting seat made from brown leather sits atop the base of the chair, which is mirrored by the surface of the accompanying table.

bodyOriginal.alt: Photo of light by Massimo Rigaglia

bodyOriginal.text: Massimo Rigaglia , a Milan-based artist and designer, created the Lights in Tension light collection from strips of flexible bamboo held in place by leather cords.
The result is a lightweight, curved structure anchored by a brass base that "embraces fragility as an aesthetic value", said Rigaglia.

bodyOriginal.alt: Photo of travertine and glass tables

bodyOriginal.text: BR Collection by Studio Alessandra Hofmann
These coffee tables by Basel-based Studio Alessandra Hofmann were informed by brutalist architecture.
The cube-shaped blocks of travertine are intersected with rectangular slabs of handmade cast glass, creating two levels to the tabletop.
The designer took an experimental approach to working with natural materials, embracing reactions created in the design process such as bubbles in the glass and open pores in the travertine.

bodyOriginal.alt: Photo of speakers by ArmoniusLab

bodyOriginal.text: Founded by designer Elia Dusi, ArmoniusLab presented its Saturnia speakers, where the audio unit is encompassed by acid-treated iron that resembles Saturn's rings.

The speaker was designed to be placed on the floor and tilt upwards, so sound travels "not directly to the listener, but around the room," the studio explained, creating a different style of listening experience.

bodyOriginal.alt: Photo of day bed by Studio YellowDot

bodyOriginal.text: Studio YellowDot collaborated with pasta company Barilla's 3D-printed pasta project Artisia to create a daybed that resembles the food's shape.
The hollow furniture, which was 3D printed in one piece from a wood fibre and bioplastic composition, features a ribbed surface similar to the pasta.
According to the studio, it responded to the festival's Borders theme by highlighting the border between food technology and design.

bodyOriginal.alt: Photo of 10-metre-long rug

bodyOriginal.text: This 10-metre-long wool rug by textile studio The Happy Few was designed to reflect the experience of walking down the street, with rectangular woven blocks resembling street tiles.
The designers sought to tell a story of seasonal changes through its colour palette, with shades of grey and blue transitioning to brown and green.

bodyOriginal.alt: Photo of room divider

bodyOriginal.text: Ceramics and furniture studio Whats Wrong Duo designed the Claustra room divider, which was informed by the soft lines and transparency found in the natural world.
Comprised of brown, purple, cream and grey hues, the furniture is made from aluminium and ceramic pieces, with the Bucharest- and Zurich-based studio also creating the glazes for the clay.
Through this design,the duo aimed to explore the boundary between a functional space divider and artistic expression.
