articles.titleOriginal: The Most Powerful Economic Productivity Lever of All Time
articles.summaryOriginal: A great deal of advocacy for the development of therapies to slow and reverse aging has moved on from a focus on reducing suffering. That the majority of the arguments now focus on economic productivity and reduced entitlement costs reflects a broad and possibly quite correct cynicism about what motivates the politicians, wealthy political influencers, and bureaucrats who collectively control the

bodyOriginal.text: A great deal of advocacy for the development of therapies to slow and reverse aging has moved on from a focus on reducing suffering. That the majority of the arguments now focus on economic productivity and reduced entitlement costs reflects a broad and possibly quite correct cynicism about what motivates the politicians, wealthy political influencers, and bureaucrats who collectively control the largest flows of funding and support in our societies. Private funding for research and development focused on longevity remains very motivated by the potential reduced suffering, and indeed the potential to reduce one's own personal suffering in the years ahead. However, the longevity industry of the recent past, and for the near future, exists in a state of tension as it attempts to make the transition from a privately supported new venture to an established field supported by the full panoply of state controlled medical systems - to be as openly and comprehensively backed by governments as cancer research and development.

Most advocates these days appear to believe that the way to make this happen is to exploit the high level of anxiety in the ruling classes of much of the world that centers around the demographic transition to ever increasing numbers of older people, and the costs of old age. The governments of the world have largely chosen to exert a great deal of control over the development and provision of medicine, to the point of it becoming an expense for them, a burden much akin to the mess that was made of pension entitlements, the creation of large enough promises of future expenditure to financially ruin the systems created to manage them. Treatments for aging are a deus ex machina that will save the system, or that is the hope being pushed into government circles by advocates attempting to achieve greater support for the development of longevity therapeutics. The realpolitik always seems somewhat shabby in full daylight when it departs utterly from the considerations of what aging does to an individual, physically and mentally. The true reason to build therapies to treat aging is because this offers the strong possibility of a very sizable reduction in human suffering and death, not because it can prop up dysfunction systems of governance.
The longevity dividend: Why governments and markets must catch up

'How much' often matters less than 'how fast'. Financial systems might comfortably accommodate a decade increase in life expectancy if it emerges gradually over half a century, but could they accommodate the same increase within 5 years? Economies are built to absorb gradual change and are much less comfortable with discontinuities. Human longevity may be approaching that kind of discontinuity . The latest scientific advances point to the emergence of what we have termed 'system-level' therapeutics capable of bringing about rapid, non-linear changes in both healthspan and lifespan trajectories, challenging the incremental paradigms that underpin current economic and demographic forecasting models. If they do, governments, healthcare systems, insurers and pension funds will have to respond to a break with history, not a continuation of it.

Public debate often treats longevity as a cost curve. That is only half the ledger. In an era of demographic ageing and stagnant economic growth forecasts, one overlooked truth is emerging: longevity science may be the most powerful economic productivity lever of all time. Governments spend billions annually on education, digital transformation and industrial innovation - all in the name of boosting national productivity. Yet few acknowledge that the single largest drag on workforce participation is declining health in midlife and beyond due to ageing. In the United States, the direct costs of chronic health conditions total around $1.1 trillion - equivalent to 5.8% of US gross domestic product (GDP). When indirect costs of lost economic productivity are included, the total costs of chronic diseases in the United States increase to $3.7 trillion - in other words, they equate to almost 20% of the US GDP.

The economic argument for longevity research is clear: targeting the root causes of ageing is not just a healthcare imperative, it is set to become a non-negotiable economic strategy. Governments should treat it as such, allocating funding accordingly and incentivising translational research , clinical trials, and public-private partnerships in this field. In the 20th century, public investment in antibiotics and vaccines changed the world. In the 21st century, ageing biology has the potential to do the same.

bodyOriginal.text: Local architecture studio Arquitectonica has shaped the MSC Cruise Terminal, the world's largest cruise terminal by size, in Miami to accommodate three ships at once.
Arquitectonica designed a slim, elongated building for the building, which processes 36,000 daily passengers through its 492,000-square-feet (45,700 square metres).

bodyOriginal.alt: Port Miami cruise terminal

bodyOriginal.text: Arquitectonica has completed the world's largest cruise terminal at Port Miami Its western end rises up to accommodate a grand lobby, with a mirrored peak rising away to hold the VIP lounges nearer the middle. The building then trails out in a thin tail, which holds embarkation and disembarkation gates.

It stretches along the easternmost tip of Dodge Island, which spans diagonally between Miami Beach and Downtown Miami and contains Port Miami, a long stretch of individual terminals that service Miami's many cruise companies.

bodyOriginal.alt: Port Miami cruise terminal

bodyOriginal.text: The building rises to four storeys at its highest point The building's linear form was partially shaped by the need for organised and efficient loading, according to the team, " with minimal overlap or delay".
" Embarkation and debarkation are vertically organised, allowing both processes to occur simultaneously with minimal overlap or delay," said the team.

bodyOriginal.alt: Largest cruise terminal

bodyOriginal.text: A grand lobby processes 36,000 daily passengers "This concept is reflected in the building's dynamic, linear form, which mirrors the directionality and movement of passengers and ships."
The terminal services ships from cruise companies MSC Cruises and Explora Journeys , both as a destination point for passengers exploring locally or cruises headed to the Caribbean.

bodyOriginal.alt: Port Miami cruise terminal by Arquitectonica

bodyOriginal.text: Biometric screening is used at security The terminal is capable of accommodating, or berthing, three full-sized ships end-to-end simultaneously. Typically, while ports may see hundreds of ships pass through them each day, a terminal is capable of handling one mega-ship at a time.

bodyOriginal.text: Inspired by shapes and movement found in nature, Pablo Luna Studio conceives of hospitality spaces, wellness retreats, and homes that sympathize with their surroundings. Rather than creating a barrier between outside and inside, the airy structures welcome foliage and the natural landscape into the overall experience, blurring the boundary between structure and environment.

The firm, based in Ubud, Bali, Indonesia, is dedicated to building with nature, incorporating sustainable materials and taking a climate-responsive approach. “Imagine a home that stays cool in summer without constant air conditioning, or warm in winter with minimal heating, simply by virtue of its design,” the studio says. “This isn’t magic; it’s the intelligent application of climate responsive architecture. It’s about leveraging natural forces like sun, wind, and rain, transforming them from challenges into design opportunities.”

bodyOriginal.text: Recent projects include the Lotus Shala in Ubud, which takes the lotus—a symbol of purity and awakening—as inspiration for an elegantly concave wooden canopy with open sides supported by posts, so that those inside feel connected to their tropical surroundings. It’s built entirely from bamboo, which is an incredibly strong yet flexible material, allowing the team to create graceful curves complemented by geometric precision.

In Sanskrit, “shala” means “home,” and the spiritual practice of yoga is complemented by purpose-built pavilion designs that encourage harmony and calm. Pablo Luna Studio’s Manta Shala is yet another example, perched on the coastline of Nusa Penida, Indonesia, with an undulating roofline that evokes the way a manta ray’s body creates a gentle, wave-like motion as it swims.
Additional projects include an eco-lodge in Uganda and numerous villas, restaurants, and wellness destinations in Bali. See more on the studio’s Instagram .

bodyOriginal.text: Sarcopenia is the name given to severe age-related loss of muscle mass and strength. This loss occurs steadily throughout later life. The present state of research into this condition is representative of aging more generally, in that while a range of quite different mechanisms all have strong supporting evidence for a meaningful contribution to sarcopenia, their relative importance to one another is unclear, how they connect to one another at the detail level is unclear, which are largely causes and which are largely consequences of one another, and their relationship to the known underlying forms of cell and tissue damage that drive aging is unclear. See the evidence for loss of muscle stem cell function to be the primary cause of sarcopenia, and surrounding discussions on that topic, for example. Here, researchers point instead to disruption of lactate metabolism in both liver and muscle tissue as the primary cause of sarcopenia; the involvement of the liver a reminder that no one tissue stands alone in the matter of aging. All organs communicate with one another and are interdependent in many different ways.

Sarcopenia is a progressive disease characterized by age-related decline in skeletal muscle force and mass. The fundamental molecular pathogenesis of sarcopenia has not yet been elucidated. Here, we show that the accumulation of lactate and intracellular acidification, lactic acidosis , in skeletal muscle owing to impaired liver-skeletal muscle lactate metabolism is the fundamental cause of sarcopenia. Systemic lactate tolerance decreased in aged mice owing to the impaired lactate processing capacity in the liver, which caused lactic acidosis in skeletal muscle.

Furthermore, pharmacological activation of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) or liver-specific activation of HIF1α improved age-associated impairment in lactate tolerance, lactic acidosis in skeletal muscle, and sarcopenia. Mechanistically, the decreased nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide level was the cause of dysregulated skeletal muscle functions due to lactic acidosis. Using mouse models , our results show lactic acidosis in skeletal muscle as a key molecular pathogenesis of sarcopenia and highlight HIF1α in the liver as a pharmacological target for sarcopenia.
Link: https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeb4011

bodyOriginal.text: Normal cell metabolism , particularly the activities of mitochondria , generates oxidizing molecules that react with proteins to disrupt their function. This damage occurs constantly, and is repaired constantly. Cells remove damaged proteins, undo oxidative changes, and make use of antioxidant enzymes such as SOD1 to prevent damage from occurring in the first place. With age, oxidation increases and becomes an important component of cell dysfunction. Here, researchers note that SOD1 itself can become oxidized and harmful, and discuss the importance of antioxidants disabled by oxidization in the growth of age-related oxidative stress in cells. The specific focus is on skin aging, but the points have relevance to all tissues.

As the body's primary barrier against environmental insults, the skin is continually exposed to oxidative stress, which may contribute to progressive proteotoxic stress. Excess reactive oxygen species (ROS) can overwhelm cellular protein-quality-control systems, promoting the accumulation of damaged and misfolded proteins, proteome instability, and eventual protein homeostasis ( proteostasis ) collapse. Superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1) , a Cu/Zn-dependent cytosolic antioxidant enzyme and key component of cellular defense against superoxide radicals, is itself vulnerable to oxidative modification. ROS-mediated post-translational oxidation of SOD1 may promote its misfolding and the formation of toxic protein species, potentially establishing a self-amplifying cycle of superoxide accumulation, further protein damage, and impaired cellular homeostasis .

In cutaneous cell types, including dermal fibroblasts and epidermal cells, these processes may be especially relevant to age-associated declines in proteostatic capacity and skin aging. This review distinguishes established skin-specific evidence from hypotheses extrapolated from other systems and synthesizes current evidence on the interplay among ROS-induced protein damage, proteostasis failure, SOD1 dysfunction, and cutaneous aging. We highlight the bidirectional relationship between proteostasis collapse and mitochondrial dysfunction , which may establish a self-reinforcing cycle of oxidative stress, cellular senescence , and chronic low-grade inflammation . These interconnected processes may converge to promote extracellular-matrix remodeling and tissue dysfunction, contributing to wrinkles, reduced elasticity, and impaired barrier function.
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.arr.2026.103351

articles.titleOriginal: Are you getting ghosted more than ever? You're not alone!
articles.summaryOriginal: It's not about you; it's about a broken business culture. Our latest Dear Boom dilemma looks at how to tackle ghosting from clients. You've spent a lot of time, effort and emotional energy forging a w...

bodyOriginal.text: It's not about you; it's about a broken business culture. Our latest Dear Boom dilemma looks at how to tackle ghosting from clients.

You've spent a lot of time, effort and emotional energy forging a working relationship. It's all going well. Then… nothing. The founder who said they loved your first concept simply vanishes. A marketing lead who's briefed you thoroughly and has promised a purchase order suddenly leaves you high and dry.

It's a horrible situation to be in. From a financial standpoint alone, it can be crippling. But more fundamentally, you also start to doubt yourself. Was the quote too high? Were the concepts lame? Did they find someone cheaper, or use AI? Did you have some food on your face during the Zoom call that everyone was too polite to point out?

Horrific, right? But here's what we've learned from our community on LinkedIn and Instagram . In 2026, ghosting has become systemic. So you shouldn't take it personally. Because it's not really about you at all.

Why silence has become the default "I've seen a lot of this so far this year, and it can feel really hollow at times," says director and cinematographer Rob Pinney . "I'm still getting a good number of approaches for new projects, but many more of those now end up with a dead email chain than before."

So what's behind the trend? "There seems to be a lot more budget hesitancy right now," Rob suggests. "And I suspect some of that is to do with clients weighing up that potential spend on video production, in my case, versus what they could do with it elsewhere, including with AI tools."

Film director Farai Dube has had similar experiences. "It's a lot of stop and start," he says. "When you're at the start of the conversation, there's actually a budget, but that's in jeopardy depending on sales and generally how much money's coming in. I get that: the part that's frustrating is keeping you on the hook. I'd rather have clarity upfront."

Yet it's not just cash-strapped clients who are guilty of ghosting. Creative director Rich Holt , for instance, complains about "recruiters who appeal for specific people to contact them—even though they're supposed to know the industry and have CVs on their desk already—and then just never reply." Director and lecturer Luke Tonge , meanwhile, calls out: "folks not replying when you invite them to speak at an event. It can hold up planning for weeks and even months."
So why does ghosting seem to be getting so much worse these days?

The fear factor Graphic designer and photo retoucher Sandrine Bascouert reckons there's something deeper going on than just laziness or poor organisation. "I think some people are afraid of communication as a whole," she says. "Ghosting has become a way to avoid normal conversations where there could be feelings hurt and disappointment."

That certainly chimes with my experience as a member of Generation X. When I first entered journalism in the 1990s, almost the entire job was phoning people. As long as you were polite and respectful, everyone was happy to chat.

By around the mid-2000s, though, I noticed that many creatives under 30 were screening their calls and wouldn't pick up if they didn't know the caller personally, even if they were actively trying to promote themselves and their work, which never made any sense to me.

Eventually I admitted defeat, and switched to email. But by the mid-2010s, many creatives were keeping their emails private—despite, again, ostensibly wanting self-promotion—and I had to start relying on social media DMs instead.

In 2026, many of those creatives are now seniors and CEOs. So it's no surprise to me that some might lack the ability to have difficult conversations, and not be willing to put in the emotional labour when times get difficult. I don't wish to generalise about an entire generation, of course. But still.

Good reason or bad actor? Poor communication skills, though, are only one reason for ghosting: there are plenty more. If we're being generous, for instance, we might assume that there's been something like a family emergency, and the other party just doesn't have the capacity to even open their inbox right now.

At the other end of the spectrum, some people can just be dicks. We've all heard of companies who interview people, ask for their ideas, and then simply steal them. There was never any job, freelance work or collaboration opportunity in the first place. It was all a scam.

Then there are those who sit somewhere in the middle, who aren't malicious, but just fail to cope. That doesn't help you , of course. As designer Nicholas Robb points out: "It starts to feel unfair after you've done a couple of calls with the stakeholders, bordering on consultation to help them scope it up. It would take 30 seconds to email back and say 'not interested + a reason why'."

Yet as an entrepreneur himself, he can also empathise. "I think business owners in particular are just so overwhelmed these days that they can't afford the time or mental space to do even that," he reflects. "So I try not to take it personally."
How we should respond Other than not beating yourself up for being ghosted, though, what can you practically do?

As a rule of thumb, designer Alexander Clark has developed a script. "After two or three of my emails go unreplied, I write this", he says, " Since I've not heard from you, I'll be pausing this and moving forward with other projects. Please let me know when you'd like to proceed or if you've changed priorities. " It usually yields a response within a day."

This is a good strategy because it removes all ambiguity. You've stopped chasing them (giving them the power) and are about to close the door (giving you the power). They have no choice but to make a decision. At this point, silence and doing nothing becomes a decision in itself.

And if that's what happens? Then move on, feeling empowered that you took control of the situation. And remember: their silence is not a poor reflection on you; it's a poor reflection on their lack of professionalism and communication skills.

Setting boundaries upfront Ultimately, prevention is always better than cure. So if you want to avoid getting ghosted, it's always good to set boundaries upfront, such as a deadline for responding to proposals. That might seem a little overbearing, but remember that clients and employers are often super-busy, and a deadline can actually be helpful for them too.

Content creator Jacob Elias Nurse offers a further suggestion: have a lot of plates spinning. "One thing I've learned from my nine months of being a full-time freelancer is that keeping busy helps you not worry too much about replies from companies that want to dangle a carrot in your face," he explains. "If you keep grinding at your craft, the money will follow."

He even finds a way to frame ghosting as a positive . As he puts it: "Their disrespect isn't a reflection of your craft or your quote. If anything, it helps you weed out who you want as a client and who you don't want as one."

Founder and creative director Kirsten Murray agrees. "A person who ghosts you is not someone you want to work with," she says. "Mutual respect and open communication make for the best creative partnerships."

So maybe that's the main takeaway. Ghosting sucks, for sure, but it's not necessarily a calamity. In fact, in the long term, it could be a good thing: saving you from a nightmare client and freeing you up to find a good'un instead.

articles.summaryOriginal: Researchers have established how a protein that is nearly absent in the literature, PTCHD4, is linked to cellular senescence. Very little previous work In most papers, after a customary discussion of […]

bodyOriginal.text: Researchers have established how a protein that is nearly absent in the literature, PTCHD4, is linked to cellular senescence .

Very little previous work In most papers, after a customary discussion of the mechanics of cellular senescence and current methods of handling it and its repercussions, the researchers go on to discuss previous work relating to the particular approach at hand. However, that does not pertain to this paper; PTCHD4 is only known as being structurally related to PTCH1, which affects the Hedgehog signaling pathway [1]. While some work has linked dysregulation of Hedgehog pathways to accelerated neurodegeneration [2], the specific role of PTCHD4 was not clear.

The researchers found that, when exposed to the genotoxin bleomycin, PTCHD4 increases alongside inflammation markers in a variety of cells, including human fetal lung diploid fibroblasts, mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs), alveolar epithelial type II cells (AEC2s), human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) and adult retinal pigment epithelial cells. Aging Atlas data confirmed this upregulation in other types of cells as well, and NCBI data listed this molecule as being disease-associated: its presence is negligible under ordinary conditions.

The team then examined young mice, old mice, and progeric mice, staining for PTCHD4 alongside the senescence biomarker p16. The two biomarkers were expressed in similar quantities among each group in multiple tissues. Similar results were found in human tissue samples; idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) patients expressed more PTCHD4 in their lungs than people without the disease, and human lung cells expressing PTCHD4 were more likely to also express established senescence markers.

Significant effects on senescence The next experiment involved creating MEFs that do not express PTCHD4 and then driving them senescent through replication. PTCHD4 was found to be a critical driver of senescence in this group; after an average of eight passages, ordinary MEFs exhibited signs of senescence, such as the key biomarker SA-β-gal, while this did not occur to the PTCHD4-deficient MEFs until an average of passage 14.

This line of experimentation continued with PTCHD4-overexpressing MEFs, which began exhibiting senescence-related features such as SA-β-gal early in passage 5. Similar results were found in AEC2s; the inflammatory biomarkers IL6 and IL8, along with SA-β-gal, were upregulated alongside PTCHD4 overexpression.

This testing continued with live mice. The researchers utilized mice that do not express PTCHD4 along with wild-type mice, and they exposed both groups to D-galactose, which mimics many of the symptoms of natural aging. The mice that did not express PTCHD4 were much more resistant to D-galactose than wild-type mice, and there were no detectable physical or biochemical problems caused by this absence.

The team then continued with naturally aging animals. They found that mice that do not express PTCHD4 naturally live months longer than wild-type mice, and mice without it apparenly do not develop white hair the way that wild-type animals do.

bodyOriginal.alt: PTCHD4 aging

bodyOriginal.text: A further experiment involved subjecting mice to bleomycin, which harms lung function in a way that mimics IPF in people. As expected, the mice exhibited features of lung fibrosis within 21 days. However, the PTCHD4-less mice suffered from fewer symptoms of the disease, retaining more lung capacity, less immune infiltration, less destruction of alveolar tissues, and less fibrosis than wild-type mice.

A well-known signaling pathway In this study, PTCHD4 was found to have no effects on the Hedgehog pathway or related genes. Instead, its effects were found to be due to AKT signaling. AKT activation normally increases with aging, but a lack of PTCHD4 diminished this. The team created MEFs that do not express PTCHD4 but express AKT through a different construct, and these MEFs were not protected by their lack of PTCHD4. Similar experiments involving the direct expression of AKT in other cell types confirmed these results, recapitulating the effects of PTCHD4.

The researchers believe that “PTCHD4 may represent a candidate target for senescence-associated interventions” and that there is “a potential role for PTCHD4 in age-related fibrotic disease.” However, this is an initial study. Further work will need to be done to confirm these results, elucidate the relationship of PTCHD4 and AKT, ascertain any side effects of eliminating or suppressing PTCHD4, and determine if PTCHD4 can be targeted by interventions.

bodyOriginal.text: A few species of hydra are immortal in their normal environmental conditions, meaning that function does not decline over time and mortality risk does not increase over time. Researchers spent a good deal of time taking care of hundreds of hydra some years ago to demonstrate that this is the case . Hydra are lower animals, essentially a bundle of stem cells capable of regenerating and replacing any part of their bodies, somewhat analogous to an ambulatory embryo. It is an open question as to whether anything we can learn from their biochemistry can be useful in human medicine.

In today's open access paper, researchers report on the employment of telomerase by hydra. Telomeres are repeated sequences at the end of chromosomes that shorten with each cell replication , creating a clock that leads to cell death when telomeres are too short. In most species, somatic cells are limited in this way in order to minimize the risk of cancer, while stem cells employ telomerase to maintain long telomeres while delivering a supply of new daughter somatic cells to replace losses. The body is just a temporary vehicle for an immortal population of germline stem cells, in one view. Hydra are obvious very different in terms of the balance between stem cell behavior versus somatic cell behavior in individuals.
Telomerase expression and activity in the immortal cnidarian Hydra

Most living eumetazoan animals are mortal. A fundamental mechanism underlying cellular and organismal aging in many species is the progressive shortening of telomeres - protective nucleoprotein structures at chromosome ends. The finite replicative lifespan of somatic cells is linked to telomere attrition. The discovery of telomerase, a ribonucleoprotein complex with reverse transcriptase activity that synthesizes telomeric repeats, provided a molecular explanation for the unlimited proliferative potential of germlines, stem cells, and most cancer cells. In humans, telomerase is not expressed in most somatic tissues and is active primarily in germ cells, stem cells, and certain rapidly renewing tissues such as blood or intestinal epithelium .

Comparative studies indicate that telomere dynamics correlate with lifespan, with slower shortening rates in long-lived species. Recent cross-species analyses, however, reveal a more complex picture, suggesting that the relationship between telomere maintenance strategies (telomerase activity vs. alternative lengthening ) and longevity is not strictly deterministic. Nevertheless, it remains a prevailing hypothesis that biologically immortal organisms must possess robust mechanisms for telomere maintenance. Supporting this, sustained telomerase activity in somatic tissues has been documented in non-senescent invertebrate models such as planarians and long-lived bivalves .

Importantly, several taxa , including some hydras, planarians, and rotifers , have been reported to exhibit negligible or undetectable senescence. In this study, we characterized the telomerase of Hydra vulgaris . The expression pattern of the telomerase catalytic subunit (hyTERT) mRNA correlates with regions exhibiting high proliferative potential and remains unchanged during budding or regeneration. These findings were further corroborated by measurements of telomerase activity. Our data suggest that telomerase may play a role in the immortality of Hydra.

articles.titleOriginal: What this elegant redesign of a sparkling water brand teaches us about packaging in 2026
articles.summaryOriginal: Antwerp studio WeWantMore's refresh of BRU trades a second-long shelf glance for a seat at the table. It's become such a cliché in packaging design, you'd think it was law. Everything needs to be opti...

bodyOriginal.text: Antwerp studio WeWantMore's refresh of BRU trades a second-long shelf glance for a seat at the table.

It's become such a cliché in packaging design, you'd think it was law. Everything needs to be optimised for that single second a shopper glances at it on a shelf. It needs to stand out from the crowd, lure people in. You only have the time it takes for a heart to beat, so don't waste it. Throw everything you have into drawing the eye.

All of which makes a lot of sense. But it's useful to remember that not every single product is fighting for attention from tired and time-poor supermarket shoppers. Sometimes, packaging needs to do very different things.

Sparkling water is a great example. Many of us go to the supermarket for the low-cost stuff, where we expect them to pile it high and sell it cheap. But when we're in a restaurant, the design of a bottle—whether it's wine or water—is an important part of the experience.
In short, we want something to visually elevate our evening out. And that's something Belgian sparkling water brand BRU, which has long been associated with fine dining, understood well.

Who is BRU? BRU can trace its origins back to the 17th century, when it started bottling the natural spring water of Stoumont, in the Ardennes. In modern times, it's been commercialised as a table water brand through the Spadel group, with a name shortened from the French word bruisser (meaning to rustle or murmur).

bodyOriginal.alt: Three framed vintage-style BRU sparkling water posters and advertisements displayed on a wood-panelled wall above a formally set dining table with white tablecloths and glassware
Blue awning above a restaurant entrance featuring BRU branding and "Some things just belong on the table" tagline, with elegant wooden doors and stone facade behind

bodyOriginal.text: What is stylish and sophisticated at one time, though, can be perceived as old-hat and boring a few decades on. And in recent years, however, BRU had become increasingly perceived in this way.

WeWantMore , a creative agency founded in Antwerp in 2006, set out to change that, repositioning it "from a restaurant staple to the finishing touch for the table, designed for every meaningful moment shared around food." An important aspect of that was shifting the focus of the packaging from trying to stand out in the shop to being something people would be proud to display on their table.

Calm and disciplined The new packaging does a great job of putting that idea into practice. The tone is calmer, with a colour palette centred around a deep navy blue that both feels refined and evokes obvious associations with water.

bodyOriginal.alt: Clear glass bottle of BRU sparkling water with blue label featuring a deer motif and blue screw cap, casting a soft shadow against a cream background
Bottle of BRU sparkling water with a redesigned label featuring a blue leaping stag and bold typography against a white background
Three bottles of BRU sparkling water with white labels featuring a navy deer logo and typography, displayed against a neutral background

bodyOriginal.text: The existing brand emblem of a leaping stag is now sleek and sculptural, while avoiding the "minimise everything down to nothing" trend that might have robbed it of all its distinctiveness. And while the lettering is colourful and decorative, it never overwhelms the label, thanks to a disciplined approach to the use of white space.

The result is a design that delivers exactly what WeWantMore set out to achieve. A bottle that people would actively want in front of them while eating, and a brand slogan, "Some things just belong on the table", to drive it all home.

Key takeaways For designers in general, I'd say there are a couple of key takeaways from this story. Firstly, don't ever assume what your design needs to do. It might seem obvious to you that something, for example, needs to stand out on the shelves, but maybe it doesn't. Maybe it won't even appear on the shelves at all.

bodyOriginal.alt: La Touche Perlée logo in white typography on a deep blue background
Bright blue sculptural stag with branching antlers in a leaping pose against a cream background
Person holding a BRU sparkling water brand card displaying the logo and tagline "Naturally sparkling, some things just belong on the table

bodyOriginal.text: Yes, we all want to dive into making cool things as soon as possible. But before you open that Photoshop document, before you start brainstorming even, you need to be absolutely sure you understand the product, the business behind it, the target audience.

The second lesson, I think, is that heritage is an asset to treasure, but rarely needs to be preserved in aspic. WeWantMore could have kept its stag exactly as it was, or completely ditched it; both approaches would probably have been disastrous.

Instead, they subtly modernised it in a way that didn't alienate fans, but would also attract new ones. That's never an easy task, but if you pull it off as a designer, the world will soon be beating a path to your door.

articles.titleOriginal: We Are Pi's ads for Interrail break free from travel cliches to show how passengers really feel
articles.summaryOriginal: This clever poster turns a sentence into a train journey: a simple but effective design trick, delivered in style. Let's be honest, we all know what a travel ad looks like. Beautiful scenery, with not...

bodyOriginal.text: This clever poster turns a sentence into a train journey: a simple but effective design trick, delivered in style.

Let's be honest, we all know what a travel ad looks like. Beautiful scenery, with not a bulldozer or screaming infant in sight? Check. Catchy yet ultimately bland and empty slogan? Check? Smiling, impossibly attractive people? Check.

Of course, there's nothing wrong with that. Holidays for most of us are just a welcome break from everyday life, and a little bit of fantasy never did anyone any harm. And I've got nothing personally against impossibly attractive people; some of my best friends count among their number.

But if you're trying to sell consumers on something they wouldn't normally do, and in fact might be nervous of doing in a foreign country where they don't speak the lingo, you'll need to work a little harder.

That's exactly the challenge that the global brand consultancy We Are Pi , working with social agency Butterfly Effect , were presented with. They were approached by Interrail B.V, the Dutch company behind the European rail travel scheme that makes it cheap and easy to travel across the continent with a special pass.

As well as boosting the scheme, there was also a bit of brand housekeeping to do. Up until this point, Interrail B.V. had two brands for essentially the same rail pass: Interrail for people living in Europe, Eurail for visitors from elsewhere. The latter needed to be folded into the Interrail brand, following the business changing its name from Eurail B.V. to Interrail B.V. earlier in the year.

Better than flying The campaign indirectly challenges the notion that because flying is quicker, it's better. Instead, it leans into the idea that the longer journey isn't an inconvenience; it's part of the adventure, via a brand concept they've dubbed The Interrail Effect.

This was backed up by a customer survey in which around 70% of Interrail customers said their trip changed how they see the world. A similar number considered the experiences more impactful than other types of travel, and around a quarter considered it much more impactful than other holidays they'd taken.

bodyOriginal.alt: Yellow train route with text labels forming the phrase "Realising the best bit is between here and there and there" overlaid on a map of Europe for Interrail campaign

bodyOriginal.text: To get this across visually, the launch poster shows a stylised map of Europe. Running across it is a single yellow line representing a train route; only the stops aren't cities – they're words. Joining them together gives you the sentence: "Realising the best bit is between here and there."
It's a common design trick, but it works because it forces the reader to make a bit of an effort. Had the sentence been instantly legible, it wouldn't make half as much impact.

There's a nice extra touch too: the journey doesn't end with the last word; the line continues, albeit it's now dotted and straight. It's a subtle way to evoke the idea of exploring and making it up as you go along, without beating people over the head with the idea.

Creator-led campaign Another element of the campaign is a series of short video clips made by 30 creators from the US, Canada, Australia and Europe, who were asked to travel across the continent with Interrail over summer and share their experiences.

These clips sit in a comfortable space between standard YouTube shorts and glossy, cinematic films. The former would have been a bit "So what?", the second would have seemed a bit overblown for a target audience that's likely to be sleeping in the cheapest hostel. The sweet spot they've reached feels, in the words of Goldilocks, just right.
Ultimately, there's nothing particularly new in this campaign, but at the same time, there didn't need to be.

As Özlem Birkalan, chief brand and commercial officer at Interrail, puts it: "'The Interrail Effect' isn't something we invented. It's something travellers have described to us for decades, in their own words, after every journey. What's changing is that we're finally building the brand around it. Not around where people travel, but around what travelling like this does to them."

The campaign launched globally on 10 September in the UK, Australia and the US, and will roll out across a mix of paid, owned and earned channels including paid media, organic social, EDM, partnerships and PR as well as participating creators' own Instagram, TikTok and other social platforms.

articles.titleOriginal: Pentagram's twin logos for Doha Design District are a masterclass in crafting sub-brands
articles.summaryOriginal: Led by Samar Maakaroun, these two identities for a maker space and event space highlight how strong brand architecture is built on discipline, not decoration. Msheireb Downtown Doha is a planned city...

bodyOriginal.text: Led by Samar Maakaroun, these two identities for a maker space and event space highlight how strong brand architecture is built on discipline, not decoration.

Msheireb Downtown Doha is a planned city in Doha, the capital of Qatar, that's designed to regenerate the historical district of Mushayrib (literally, 'a place to drink water' in Arabic). It's been promoted as being the world's first sustainable downtown regeneration project, and one of the smartest cities on Earth. And Doha Design District (DDD) is its hub for design, innovation, and collaboration.

Director Dana Kazic approached Samar Maakaroun and her team at Pentagram with a challenge: introduce two distinct spaces within the district, while strengthening, rather than fragmenting, the parent brand.

One would be a maker's space dedicated to experimentation and artistic development; the other, an event space that becomes a destination for exhibitions, events, and public engagement. They'd be positioned physically opposite each other.

Striving for connection It sounds like either a massive challenge or the stuff of nightmares, depending on how much experience you've had dealing with having to juggle the competing demands of brands and sub-brands, not to mention different languages.

In these scenarios, the client typically wants the two sub-brand spaces to feel connected. But in practice, they often get two names that share a typeface and a colour palette, but not much else. The connection is clearly expressed in a brand guideline PDF, yet never really translates to what the public actually sees and feels.

bodyOriginal.alt: Pentagram's dual logos for Doha Design District showing Sada in orange and Mada in turquoise, split typographically down the middle
Black carrier bag with orange handles and Sada branding, displayed on a white surface in studio lighting
Mada storefront with turquoise signage and logo on white and black facade, with a blurred figure walking past

bodyOriginal.text: To avoid that scenario, Samar—whose identity for The Mosaic Rooms in London we covered back in April—and her team took the time to get things right. As they put it: "The relationship had to allow equity to move in all directions: from DDD to the sub-brands, between the sub-brands themselves, between languages, and back again into the wider district."

Naming and letter design Next up came the naming process. The team explored a range of ideas, from letter repetitions connected to the DDD symbol to Arabic words that had a spatial dimension and were easy to say out loud. The main thing was that the names needed to work together naturally and feel like two halves of a whole.

They found the solution in a pair of Arabic words that already had a relationship with each other. Mada, meaning range, reach or possibility, was chosen for the maker's space. Sada, meaning echo, was chosen for the space where finished work meets an audience.

bodyOriginal.alt: Four illuminated turquoise and black signage panels for Doha Design District displaying the mada maker space and event space branding on a white wall

bodyOriginal.text: From a visual point of view, "sada" and "mada" are built from almost identical letterforms, mirrored and rearranged, rather than drawn from scratch as two separate typefaces. Or to put it another way, one looks like the echo of another. This means the relationship between the two spaces doesn't need to be hammered home: it's immediately, instinctively obvious.

At a deeper level, there's a sense of culture and history baked into their DNA. Both names carry the letter D, which has been lifted from the existing Doha Design District symbol, while the other letterforms are inspired by the architecture of Msheireb, the downtown Doha district the whole scheme sits within.

Again, this works elegantly in making the whole brand architecture work harmoniously together. Every curve and notch in the wordmarks echoes something structural in the area, making them feel like a natural part of their surroundings, rather than something tagged on.

Key takeaway Here's what I think anyone working on a sub-brand can learn from this. It's terribly easy, especially when you're on a tight deadline, to go with the obvious solutions to making multiple brands work together. Use the same typeface, the same colour, the same grid system. And bosh! You have a unified system. Well, kinda.

bodyOriginal.alt: Neon green pixelated text and geometric shapes displayed on a black screen with cyan border, installed in a minimalist corridor with warm-lit alcoves on either side

bodyOriginal.text: This approach might look good in a presentation, but in the real world, where your designs are having to live, breathe and do their work, they run the risk of looking like an afterthought, stapled on to the parent brand rather than being an organic part of it.

What Pentagram did here was different. Rather than seeing the existing brand at surface level—the type, the colours—they delved deep into its ethos instead, and located the connective tissue that would make the new sub-brands feel naturally part of it.
The result? No one has to stand there explaining that Sada and Mada are part of the Doha Design District. It's just obvious. And that's the job.

articles.titleOriginal: Lung Fibrosis Drug Lowers Biological Age Estimates
articles.summaryOriginal: Six different aging clocks detected younger blood protein profiles in patients taking the experimental lung-fibrosis drug rentosertib. This suggests possible anti-aging […]

bodyOriginal.text: Six different aging clocks detected younger blood protein profiles in patients taking the experimental lung-fibrosis drug rentosertib. This suggests possible anti-aging effects, but separating those from the narrower benefits of treating fibrosis remains a challenge [1].

The AI-developed drug Many drugs developed for particular diseases act on aging-related biological processes. That creates an opportunity: a clinical trial could investigate both whether a drug treats its intended disease and whether it has broader effects on aging. Ordinary clinical measurements cannot establish those broader effects, but we now have biological age clocks that closely track chronological age or predict mortality risk [2]. These clocks have been used in numerous trials as proxies to estimate the intervention’s effect on aging.

In a new study published in Nature Biotechnology , the researchers analyzed blood samples from a Phase 2a trial whose results were published last year [3]. That 12-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested rentosertib, an inhibitor of the kinase TNIK, which has been implicated in several aging-related processes [4].

Rentosertib was developed by the longevity biotech company Insilico, using a proprietary AI-based drug discovery platform, to treat idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), a progressive disease in which excessive scar tissue compromises lung function. IPF is age-related, with a mean age of onset around 65 years, and aging processes such as cellular senescence and inflammation are heavily involved.
The new analysis included 42 of the trial’s 71 participants. Alongside placebo, the trial tested three regimens: 30 milligrams once daily, 30 milligrams twice daily, and 60 milligrams once daily.

Lower biological age readings The researchers used six different proteomic clocks, which analyze protein levels in blood. The proteomic clocks’ appeal is partly interpretability: researchers can identify which proteins affect the readings and connect them to known biological processes more directly than is often possible with methylation-based clocks. The clocks were developed by different teams, using data from UK Biobank, including one clock developed by Insilico itself. Four of the clocks were trained on chronological age, and two on mortality.

All six clocks detected lower predicted biological ages in patients taking rentosertib, although not at every dose or visit. After four weeks, the four chronological age-based clocks rated patients taking 60 milligrams once daily (the single-dose regimen) roughly three years younger, on average, than at the start of treatment. These changes were statistically significant compared with placebo. However, the two clocks trained to predict mortality risk did not show a significant change at that dose at week four.

Patients taking 30 milligrams twice daily (the split-dose regimen) showed the most consistent decreases across both types of clocks. The largest reductions in predicted biological age appeared by week four, with little additional change over the remaining eight weeks.

These results essentially mean that patients’ blood protein profiles became more similar to those associated with younger people. They do not, however, establish that the treated patients regained years of youth or would live longer.

Is there a broad anti-aging effect? Looking beyond the clock readings, the researchers found that treatment changed the levels of 326 blood proteins, including proteins involved in fibrosis, metabolism, and cellular stress responses. Most changes in the two higher-dose groups persisted throughout the trial or appeared later in treatment, suggesting that the drug continued affecting patients’ biology even after predicted ages plateaued.

The researchers then examined which proteins contributed most to the younger age estimates. A fibrosis-associated protein, LTBP2, stood out as a major contributor. It was used by all six clocks, which raises the question of whether their agreement mainly reflects the drug’s effect on fibrosis, rather than broader slowing of aging.

To explore whether the lower age estimates reflected more than improvement in fibrosis, the researchers compared changes in predicted age with changes in lung function. The two did not closely track each other. This suggests that improved lung function alone might not explain the clock changes, although lung function does not capture every aspect of IPF.

The team then compared the treatment-induced protein changes with differences between younger and older participants in UK Biobank. With the split dose, proteins associated with aging tended to move in the opposite direction: those found at higher levels in older people tended to decrease, and vice versa. This pattern was not statistically significant with the single daily dose.

Finally, the researchers examined proteins associated with cellular senescence. These proteins tended to increase in the placebo group but decrease with treatment, suggesting that rentosertib might reduce senescence-associated activity, although the researchers did not directly measure senescent cells in tissues.

These findings strengthen the case for investigating rentosertib as a potential geroprotector. However, because fibrosis, metabolism, and senescence are closely connected, they still cannot definitively establish whether the drug affects aging beyond its benefits for IPF.

“This study illustrates how biomarkers of aging can be incorporated into conventional clinical trials,” Vadim Gladyshev, a professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School and a coauthor of the study, told Lifespan News. “If validated more broadly, such approaches could allow us to learn not only whether a treatment affects a particular disease, but also whether it influences some aspects of aging biology.”

articles.titleOriginal: From World Cup Champions to Longevity Champions
articles.summaryOriginal: Fresh from Spain’s spectacular victory in the 2026 FIFA World Cup, Madrid is preparing for another kind of world-class gathering: one focused not on winning more […]

bodyOriginal.text: Fresh from Spain’s spectacular victory in the 2026 FIFA World Cup, Madrid is preparing for another kind of world-class gathering: one focused not on winning more years of sporting glory, but on winning more healthy years of life.

On September 30 and October 1, 2026, the International Longevity Summit Madrid 2026 will bring together leading scientists, physicians, entrepreneurs, investors and futurists to explore one of humanity’s greatest challenges—and potentially greatest opportunities: extending healthy human life.

Organized by the International Longevity Alliance, the Summit comes to a city uniquely positioned to lead the global conversation on longevity. Spain has the highest life expectancy in the European Union, while the Comunidad de Madrid has recorded the highest life expectancy of any EU region, reaching the remarkable landmark of 85.7 years according to Eurostat. Madrid may therefore be more than simply a great European capital; it could increasingly be considered a “Blue Zone 2.0”: a modern, dynamic metropolis where exceptional longevity meets cutting-edge science, biotechnology and innovation.

bodyOriginal.alt: LSM 2

bodyOriginal.text: And now, after Spain’s national team, La Roja, captured the 2026 FIFA World Cup, Spain can proudly claim another world-leading achievement. In July, Spain defeated Argentina 1–0 after extra time to win its second men’s World Cup title, adding a new chapter to a country already renowned for its health, lifestyle and longevity.

From world champions on the football field to potential champions of healthy longevity, Spain is demonstrating that the future may belong to those who know how to live—and perhaps someday live much longer.

bodyOriginal.alt: LSM 3

bodyOriginal.text: A new royal home at Spain’s most prestigious medical institution After the success of previous editions held at the Ilustre Colegio Oficial de Médicos de Madrid (ICOMEM), where the Summit was inaugurated with the participation of the Mayor of Madrid, José Luis Martínez-Almeida, the 2026 edition takes a major institutional step forward.

This year, the Summit will be held at the magnificent Real Academia Nacional de Medicina de España (RANME), the Royal National Academy of Medicine of Spain, the country’s most prestigious medical institution. Founded in 1734, the Academy occupies a unique place in Spanish scientific history. The Academy is under the High Patronage of His Majesty King Felipe VI, underlining the exceptional institutional importance of the venue. The Academy is also historically associated with some of the greatest names in medicine, including Spain’s Nobel laureates Santiago Ramón y Cajal and Severo Ochoa.

Located in the historic heart of Madrid, between the Royal Palace and the Teatro Real, the RANME will provide an extraordinary setting for a conversation that could reshape the future of medicine itself.

From George Church and Ray Kurzweil to Eric Topol and Peter Diamandis The International Longevity Summit has rapidly become a meeting point for some of the world’s most influential thinkers in longevity, biotechnology, medicine and the future of humanity.

Previous editions of the International Longevity Summit in Madrid have featured an exceptional roster of speakers, including George Church , pioneering geneticist; Ray Kurzweil , futurist and inventor; Steve Horvath , creator of the epigenetic clock; Andrea Maier , longevity physician and researcher; Mehmood Khan , global health and life sciences leader; Liz Parrish , biotechnology entrepreneur; Aubrey de Grey , biomedical gerontologist; Bryan Johnson , entrepreneur and longevity pioneer; María Blasco , molecular biologist and telomere researcher; João Pedro de Magalhães , biogerontologist and aging researcher; and Michael Ringel , biotechnology and pharmaceutical executive—along with many other leading scientists, physicians, entrepreneurs, and innovators from around the world.

The 2026 edition continues and expands this tradition of quality. Among the distinguished participants and speakers announced for 2026 are Eric Topol , cardiologist and digital medicine pioneer; Peter Diamandis , entrepreneur and futurist; Brian Kennedy , aging researcher; Valentin Fuster , cardiologist and cardiovascular scientist; Bashayer Almubarak , longevity and health innovation leader; Guido Kroemer , cell biologist and aging researcher; Steven Austad , biogerontologist; Michel Poulain , demographer and Blue Zones researcher; Michael West , stem cell pioneer; Mike Chan , longevity expert and entrepreneur; Wei-Wu He , biotechnology entrepreneur; Patrick E. Sewell , longevity physician; Ronald Bonilla , dentist and longevity innovator; Tina Woods , health and longevity leader; Daniel Wallerstorfer , geneticist and biotech entrepreneur; David Wood , futurist and longevity advocate; and Kenneth Scott , entrepreneur and longevity advocate—along with many other leading international and Spanish scientists, physicians, entrepreneurs, and innovators.

The program will span the biology of aging, rejuvenation biotechnology, preventive and regenerative medicine, artificial intelligence, health data, biomarkers, the longevity economy and the profound social consequences of potentially dramatic increases in human healthspan.

From conference to scientific marketplace: posters and startup pitches debut in 2026 For the first time, the International Longevity Summit will introduce scientific poster sessions and startup pitches, opening the stage to a new generation of researchers, entrepreneurs and innovators. Through an international Open Call, selected participants will have the opportunity to present research projects, scientific posters, short talks and startup initiatives to an audience of experts, investors, physicians and longevity enthusiasts. The goal is to make the Summit not only a place where established leaders discuss the future, but also a platform where the next generation of breakthroughs, companies and scientific careers can begin.

A distinguished group of prestigious Spanish and international institutions is supporting this historic event, organized by International Longevity Alliance (ILA) at the Royal National Academy of Medicine of Spain (RANME) , in collaboration with the Official College of Physicians of Madrid (ICOMEM) and Madrid Innovation . International supporters include European Wellness and Triple Helix Science at the Gold level, as well as Novogenia and Nesa World at the Silver level. The event is also endorsed by leading foundations and organizations, including HealthGevity Nation, Hevolution Foundation, Human Longevity Inc., HumanityPlus, Immortalis, KHL Foundation, Life Extension Foundation, Lifeboat Foundation, Longevity Escape Velocity Foundation, Millennium Project, XPRIZE Foundation , together with innovative companies such as Cenegenics , GERO , and OXANA . This year, the Summit will also welcome a new generation of startups working in healthtech, healthcare innovation and longevity, with the logistical support of CRRATE and StartUp Olé Salamanca .
The 2026 edition aims to further strengthen Madrid’s role as a bridge between Europe, Latin America, North America and the rapidly expanding global longevity economy.

bodyOriginal.text: Two days of UNESCO history before exploring the future The Summit will begin even before the scientific program officially opens. On September 28 and 29, participants will be able to join two special pre-conference excursions to some of the most remarkable UNESCO World Heritage sites surrounding Madrid. The first day will travel south-east to Alcalá de Henares, Aranjuez and Toledo . The second will head north-west to Ávila, Segovia and El Escorial .

The contrast is intentional: participants will explore centuries of Spanish and European history before returning to Madrid to discuss technologies that may transform the future of human life itself. From ancient cathedrals and royal palaces to cellular rejuvenation, artificial intelligence and longevity escape velocity, the International Longevity Summit 2026 promises a journey through both humanity’s past and its possible future.

This summer, Spain has shown the world how to win on the football field. This autumn, Madrid will invite the world to explore how humanity might also win the greatest matches of all: the race against aging!

bodyKo: 2026년 FIFA 월드컵에서 스페인이 화려하게 우승한 직후, 마드리드는 또 다른 세계적 수준의 모임을 준비하고 있다. 이는 스포츠 영광의 연장이 아니라 건강한 삶의 시간을 더 많이 얻는 데 초점을 맞춘 것이다.
2026년 9월 30일과 10월 1일, 국제 롱제비티 서밋 마드리드 2026이 선도적인 과학자, 의사, 기업가, 투자자, 미래학자들을 한자리에 모아 인류의 가장 큰 도전 중 하나이자 잠재적으로 가장 큰 기회인 건강한 인간 생명 연장을 탐구할 예정입니다.

국제 롱제비티 연합이 주최하는 이번 정상회의는 롱제비티에 관한 글로벌 대화를 이끌 독특한 위치에 있는 도시에서 개최됩니다. 스페인은 유럽연합에서 가장 높은 기대수명을 기록하고 있으며, 마드리드 자치구는 유로스타트에 따르면 85.7세라는 놀라운 기록을 세우며 EU 지역 중 가장 높은 기대수명을 기록했습니다. 따라서 마드리드는 단순한 유럽 수도를 넘어설 수 있습니다; 점점 더 '블루 존 2.0'으로 간주될 수 있습니다: 뛰어난 롱제비티가 첨단 과학, 생명공학, 혁신과 만나는 현대적이고 역동적인 대도시입니다.
그리고 이제 스페인 국가대표팀 라 로하가 2026년 FIFA 월드컵을 차지한 후, 스페인은 또 하나의 세계 최고 성과를 자랑스럽게 주장할 수 있게 되었습니다. 7월에는 연장전 끝에 아르헨티나를 1-0으로 꺾고 두 번째 남자 월드컵 우승을 차지하며, 이미 건강, 라이프스타일, 롱제비티로 유명한 나라에 새로운 장을 열었습니다.
축구장의 세계 챔피언부터 건강한 롱제비티의 잠재적 챔피언까지, 스페인은 미래가 살아가는 법을 아는 이들에게 속할 수 있음을 보여주고 있으며, 언젠가는 훨씬 더 오래 살지도 모른다는 것을 보여주고 있습니다.
스페인에서 가장 권위 있는 의학 기관의 새로운 왕실 거처 마드리드 공식 의학 학교(ICOMEM)에서 개최된 이전 대회들의 성공에 힘입어, 마드리드 시장 호세 루이스 마르티네스-알메이다가 참석한 가운데 정상회의가 개막되었고, 2026년 대회는 제도적으로 중요한 진전을 이루었습니다.

올해 정상회의는 스페인 왕립 의학 아카데미(RANME)인 스페인 왕립 의학 아카데미에서 개최됩니다. 1734년에 설립된 이 아카데미는 스페인 과학사에서 독특한 위치를 차지하고 있습니다. 아카데미는 펠리페 6세 국왕의 고위 후원 아래 있어 이 장소의 탁월한 제도적 중요성을 강조합니다. 또한 아카데미는 스페인의 노벨상 수상자인 산티아고 라몬 이 카할과 세베로 오초아 등 의학계의 위대한 인물들과도 역사적으로 연관되어 있습니다.
마드리드의 역사적인 중심부, 왕궁과 테아트로 레알 사이에 위치한 RNME는 의학의 미래를 재구성할 수 있는 대화를 위한 특별한 무대를 제공할 것입니다.
조지 처치와 레이 커즈와일, 에릭 토폴, 피터 디아만디스에 이르기까지, 국제 롱제비티 정상회의는 롱제비티, 생명공학, 의학, 인류의 미래 분야에서 세계에서 가장 영향력 있는 사상가들이 만나는 장소가 되었습니다.

마드리드에서 열린 이전 국제 롱제비티 서밋 대회에는 뛰어난 연사들이 참여했으며, 여기에는 선구적인 유전학자 조지 처치; 미래학자이자 발명가인 레이 커즈와일; 후성유전 시계의 창시자인 스티브 호르바스; 롱제비티 의사이자 연구자인 안드레아 마이어; 글로벌 보건 및 생명과학 분야의 리더 메흐무드 칸; 생명공학 기업가 리즈 패리시; 생의학 노인학자 오브리 드 그레이; 브라이언 존슨, 기업가이자 롱제비티 개척자; 마리아 블라스코, 분자생물학자이자 텔로미어 연구자; 조앙 페드로 데 마갈랴이스, 생물노인학자이자 노화 연구자; 그리고 마이클 링겔, 생명공학 및 제약 경영자—그리고 전 세계의 많은 선도적인 과학자, 의사, 기업가, 혁신가들이 함께합니다.

2026년 대회는 이러한 품질 전통을 이어가고 확장합니다. 2026년 발표된 저명한 참가자 및 연사로는 심장학자이자 디지털 의학 선구자인 에릭 토폴; 기업가이자 미래학자인 피터 디아만디스; 노인 연구자 브라이언 케네디; 심장학자 및 심혈관 과학자 발렌틴 푸스터; 롱제비티 및 건강 혁신 리더인 바샤예 알무바라크; 세포생물학자이자 노화 연구자인 귀도 크로머; 생물노인학자 스티븐 오스타드; 인구학자 및 블루존 연구자 미셸 풀랭; 줄기세포 개척자 마이클 웨스트; 마이크 찬, 롱제비티 전문가이자 기업가; 웨이우 허, 생명공학 기업가; 패트릭 E. 수웰, 롱제비티 의사; 로널드 보닐라, 치과의사이자 롱제비티 혁신가; 티나 우즈, 건강 및 롱제비티 리더; 다니엘 월러스토퍼, 유전학자이자 생명공학 기업가; 미래학자이자 롱제비티 옹호자 데이비드 우드; 그리고 기업가이자 롱제비티 옹호자 케네스 스콧 등 많은 국제적·스페인 저명한 과학자, 의사, 기업가, 혁신가들이 함께합니다.
이 프로그램은 노화 생물학, 회춘 생명공학, 예방 및 재생 의학, 인공지능, 건강 데이터, 바이오마커, 롱제비티 경제, 그리고 인간 건강수명의 극적인 증가가 초래하는 심오한 사회적 영향을 아우릅니다.

컨퍼런스에서 과학 마켓플레이스: 포스터와 스타트업 피치 2026년 공개 국제 롱제비티 서밋은 처음으로 과학 포스터 세션과 스타트업 피치를 도입하여 새로운 세대의 연구자, 기업가, 혁신가들에게 무대를 열 것입니다. 국제 공개 모집을 통해 선정된 참가자들은 전문가, 투자자, 의사, 롱제비티 애호가 청중 앞에서 연구 프로젝트, 과학 포스터, 짧은 강연, 스타트업 이니셔티브를 발표할 기회를 갖게 됩니다. 목표는 서밋을 기존 리더들이 미래를 논의하는 장소일 뿐만 아니라, 차세대 혁신, 기업, 과학 경력이 시작될 수 있는 플랫폼으로 만드는 것입니다.

스페인 왕립의학아카데미(RANME)에서 국제롱제비티 연합(ILA)이 마드리드 공식 의사 협회(ICOMEM) 및 마드리드 혁신과 협력하여 주최한 이 역사적인 행사는 스페인 및 국제 기관들의 저명한 그룹이 지원합니다. 국제 후원자로는 골드 등급의 유럽 웰니스와 트리플 헬릭스 사이언스, 그리고 실버 등급의 노보제니아와 네사 월드가 있습니다. 이 행사는 HealthGevity Nation, Hevolution Foundation, 휴먼 롱제비티 Inc., 휴머니티플러스, 이모탈리스, KHL 재단, 라이프 익스텐션 재단, 라이프보트 재단, 롱제비티 이스케이프 벨로시티 재단, 밀레니엄 프로젝트, XPRIZE 재단 등 주요 재단 및 단체들의 지지를 받고 있으며, Cenegenics, GERO, OXANA와 같은 혁신적인 기업들도 함께합니다. 올해 서밋에는 CRRATE와 StartUp Olé Salamanca의 물류 지원을 받아 헬스테크, 헬스케어 혁신, 롱제비티 분야에서 활동하는 신세대 스타트업도 환영할 예정입니다.
2026년 대회는 마드리드가 유럽, 라틴 아메리카, 북미와 빠르게 성장하는 글로벌 롱제비티 경제 사이의 다리 역할을 더욱 강화하는 것을 목표로 합니다.

미래를 탐구하기 전 이틀간의 유네스코 역사 서밋이 과학 프로그램이 공식적으로 시작되기 전에 시작됩니다. 9월 28일과 29일에는 참가자들이 마드리드 주변의 가장 주목할 만한 유네스코 세계유산지들을 방문하는 두 차례의 특별 사전 소풍에 참여할 수 있습니다. 첫째 날은 남동쪽으로 알칼라 데 에나레스, 아란후에스, 톨레도를 향해 이동합니다. 둘째 날은 북서쪽으로 아빌라, 세고비아, 엘 에스코리알로 향합니다.
이 대비는 의도된 것으로, 참가자들은 수세기에 걸친 스페인과 유럽의 역사를 탐구한 뒤 마드리드로 돌아가 인간 삶의 미래를 바꿀 수 있는 기술에 대해 논의할 것입니다. 고대 대성당과 왕궁부터 세포 재생, 인공지능, 롱제비티 탈출 속도에 이르기까지, 국제 롱제비티 서밋 2026은 인류의 과거와 가능한 미래를 모두 여행할 것을 약속합니다.
올여름, 스페인은 축구장에서 승리하는 법을 세계에 보여주었다. 이번 가을, 마드리드는 인류가 가장 위대한 경기, 즉 노화와의 경주에서 어떻게 이길 수 있을지 세계에 초대할 것이다!

articles.titleOriginal: Calcium Mishandling Contributes to Muscle Loss
articles.summaryOriginal: Researchers have discovered and explained how calcium mishandling in muscle cells leads to long-term muscle weakness in older people. Calcium is not just for bones Skeletal muscle cells use calcium ions to control how and when they contract. […]

bodyOriginal.text: Researchers have discovered and explained how calcium mishandling in muscle cells leads to long-term muscle weakness in older people .

Calcium is not just for bones Skeletal muscle cells use calcium ions to control how and when they contract. This activity is modulated by CaMKII, a protein kinase that also regulates muscle adaptations in response to exercise [1] and serves a great many unrelated functions throughout multiple other tissues.

In young tissues, this system works well, with exercise producing reactive oxygen species (ROS) that are used to stimulate muscle growth [1]. However, with aging, this falls apart in multiple ways: calcium ions leak out of where they are supposed to be [2], mitochondria and calcium become uncoupled [3], and, as has been well-known for decades, ROS and oxidative damage are no longer properly mitigated [4]. The authors hypothesized that CaMKII signaling is involved in this dysregulation.

Constant expression weakens muscles In their first experiment, the researchers examined the muscles of 3.7-month-old mice and compared them to those of 33-month-old mice; 33 months is exceptionally old for a mouse, and mice of that age were provided by the gerontologist Dr. Rafael deCabo. These elderly mice had significantly smaller muscles than the younger group, substantially more CaMKII in muscle tissue, and more evidence of CaMKII activity while at rest. However, the researchers noted that the biomarker they used to detect activity, pT287-CaMKII, is not entirely consistent in various muscle tissues and CaMKII can be modified in many other ways [5].

To determine the effects of constant CAMKII activity in muscle, this team developed a adeno-associated virus (AAV) that caused it to become active only in that tissue. This AAV had local effects, meaning that the researchers were able to inject it onto only one tibialis anterior muscle of each individual mouse; the identical muscle on the other side was injected with a simple fluorescent reporter protein with no significant effects. Interestingly, feedback mechanisms caused natural CAMKII to be suppressed in the muscles that were given this artificial CAMKII increase.

Within less than two months, this increase in constant CaMKII caused the targeted muscles to shrink and become pound-for-pound weaker than the unmodified muscles in the same mice; direct stimulation at multiple frequencies found that the targeted muscles were unable to exert nearly as much force. While it did not impact total mitochondrial number, it had significant negative effects on mitochondrial organization. A similar experiment with a different cohort of mice found that, after nine months, the loss of muscle mass became even more significant.

Some of this muscle loss was found to be driven by inflammation. Blocking the inflammatory signal NF-κB while activating CaMKII blunted some of the effects; the muscles in this group did not become pound-for-pound weaker, but they still lost mass.

Age-related gene expression changes Gene expression was also significantly impacted. While there were some differences, the impact of constant CaMKII expression was broadly similar to that of natural aging in muscle, and the researchers identified many biochemical pathways that are increased both by natural aging and by increased CaMKII. Most notably, iron-handling pathways were significantly disrupted by CaMKII.

The researchers also injected naturally aged mice with CN19o, which inhibits CaMKII; while individual genes were not significantly affected, the sum total of gene expression was found to move towards a more youthful phenotype. While it did not increase muscle size in 21-month-old mice, suppressing CaMKII in these mice increased their ability to contract.

The researchers hold that age-related constant CaMKII signaling is a significant contributor to sarcopenia. In youth, this signaling is beneficial, but in an aged environment, it is apparently doing more harm than good. However, the researchers did not experimentally validate why constant CaMKII activation has the mitochondrial effects it does, nor did they fully elucidate the connection between calcium and iron signaling. Further work will need to be done to determine if CaMKII is a useful target in people.

articles.titleOriginal: Whistles marks 50 years by casting 50 customers found through mysterious fly-posters across London
articles.summaryOriginal: Weirdo helped the British fashion brand swap the usual models for "open-minded" women aged 19 to 72, found via guerrilla posters, shot in a single day and backed by new positioning and a sig...

bodyOriginal.text: Weirdo helped the British fashion brand swap the usual models for "open-minded" women aged 19 to 72, found via guerrilla posters, shot in a single day and backed by new positioning and a signature colour called Lemonade.

Fashion is a beloved passion of mine. I've always loved dressing up. I have fond memories of Topshop and Tammy Girl in my teens, and of watching The Clothes Show every Sunday evening with my mam, while my dad disappeared upstairs to tinker on the computer.

Brands like Whistles came much later. It was always considered pricey and high-end compared to other high street stores, so we never shopped there. As soon as I started earning my own money, though, I saved every penny to get the latest cuts. I remember one pair of black trousers that I treated like a precious treasure for years, until they finally went to the charity shop, battered but well-loved.

My girlfriends share similar stories. We have emotional connections to the places we once worshipped every Saturday, returning home loaded down with shopping bags. For me, it was "going up Hanley Duck" on the No.20 bus to the Potteries shopping centre. And Whistles was one of the concessions in Debenhams. Most likely the first place I looked.

Fast forward to today, and I've not given it much thought in a long while. My go-to brands these days are a mix of Japanese menswear and eye-wateringly expensive garments from Studio Nicholson or Soeur. (I've been banned from Redchurch Street. Never let me go there. Seriously.) But hey, I justify the cost by saying it's what helps me feel good rather than reaching for Botox like so many women my age are (I just can't quite bring myself to do it, even though the pressure is real). Anyway, I digress.

Whistles, would you believe, turns 50 this year (gulp) and it wanted to mark the occasion. Instead of turning to models or going through its archives, it fly-posted much of London with cryptic posters asking for "open-minded women". There was no explanation or brand mention, just a call to say what open-mindedness means to you. Remarkably, more than 2,000 people replied.

bodyOriginal.alt: Man in orange shirt wearing headphones leans against doorframe in Whistles campaign poster displayed in London Underground station with passing train
Woman in black dress standing against brick wall on London Underground platform with Whistles advertisement displaying yellow "WHISTLES" text

bodyOriginal.text: The posters were the brainchild of Weirdo, the London creative agency founded in 2021 by former pro athlete Louis Persent, which has since built a reputation for putting real people at the centre of campaigns for the likes of Arsenal, Bumble, and Snapchat. Whistles and Weirdo whittled the replies down to 50 women, aged between 19 and 72, most of whom had never modelled before. They were then photographed in a single day wearing the latest Whistles collection, set against a plain white backdrop, and each was interviewed about her life for social and film content.

Six of those women front the launch, including a BAFTA-winning documentary filmmaker, a mother and an entrepreneur. Fashion photographer Alice Neale shot them, and Archi Shah filmed them, mostly using a camcorder. The result is a two-minute film that goes out today across out-of-home, social, digital and in-store. This isn't the glossy campaign you'd expect in The Bible (that's Vogue to anyone who doesn't know). More nostalgic and raw, taking me back to those beloved shopping days in Stoke.

Along with the campaign, Weirdo has also evolved the Whistles identity, now positioned as "Designed for an Open Mind". Ah, that makes sense. And there's a new signature citrus colour called Lemonade, plus an overall tone that's described as "sharp and light".

"We're leaving behind rigid top-down campaigns and moving towards projects and commissions," says Louis. "It's an open approach to brand-building that's allowed us to shoot 50 women in one day, commission a friend group to shoot a summer collection on a trip to Athens, and have a pipeline of future projects that will keep exploring what it means to be designed for an open mind."

Speaking of the Athens shoot, it was one of a year's worth of pilot projects where a real bunch of mates shot the summer collection on holiday. Nice to see Whistles not going down the AI route like other high street retailers might be. That authenticity will do them proud, no doubt. And give my fashion industry pals a sigh of relief.

bodyOriginal.alt: Woman in burgundy leather jacket with sheepskin collar and blue jeans crouching against a bright yellow wall

bodyOriginal.text: All this was certainly needed because I'd almost forgotten about Whistles. It had felt a little tired in recent years. And the quality had dropped. Other brands came along like Cos and Uniqlo, and we women moved on. We talk, I'm afraid, and the conversation always goes like "they used to be good... try this other shop instead" (Mumsnet is brilliant for that sort of advice).

Brand loyalty is a brutal game. I can't imagine the pressure to stay relevant and loved. And brands that lose their way can always make a comeback. Just look at Topshop. A change of hands or marketing strategy can be a good thing.

When I watched the campaign film, I got quite emotional listening to the stories. So many resonated. It frightens me to think of how long ago those teenage shopping trips were, so seeing Whistles honour women like us, and our life experiences, felt very honest. Like it's capturing a collective mood.
Whether it brings me back through their doors (or onto their website), the jury's out. But it's a clever reminder of something we once loved, and that it might be worth visiting again.

articles.titleOriginal: Comparing the Responsiveness of Epigenetic Aging Biomarkers
